chapters.title: A Timetable in Blue Ink
pages: At 16.08, according to the itinerary Isabel Morgan had written in blue ink, she would leave Brno. At 19.41 she would change at Rosenstadt. At 20.03 she would board the night train west, sleep for six hours, and arrive in time for a nine o’clock meeting about a book she had not yet been commissioned to write. The plan occupied one neat page in her notebook, with the platform numbers underlined twice.

At 16.08 the train remained outside Brno, stopped between two fields under a sky the colour of old tin. Rain travelled sideways across the windows. The carriage lights shivered each time the wind struck, and a child in the next compartment asked his father whether the train had forgotten where it was going.
‘No,’ the father said. ‘It’s waiting.’
Isabel looked down at her itinerary. Waiting was not one of its verbs.

She was twenty-nine, British, and sufficiently experienced in travel to know that a schedule was a proposal rather than a promise. She also knew that knowing this did not stop her making schedules. For the last three days she had crossed Central Europe with the patient efficiency of someone carrying a glass of water through a crowded room. Her luggage fitted into a small case; her notes were divided by city; her phone displayed the route in a clean blue line.

Beneath the itinerary, in smaller writing, she had recorded the other facts she preferred to keep from the main page: the call from Adrian, two weeks earlier, in which he had said he could not continue being the person who always waited for her to come home; the email from the publisher on Monday, saying that the proposal was not quite right for their list; and the reply she had sent to both, concise and courteous.

The reply to Adrian had been, I understand. The reply to the publisher had been, Thank you for letting me know. She had then bought a ticket across Europe, as though movement could be presented as an answer without having to be one.

At 18.26 the train began moving. Nobody applauded, but several people sighed with the same embarrassed relief. Isabel bought coffee from the trolley. It tasted of hot metal and had travelled less than she had. She drank it anyway, then used the time to prepare for the meeting: a short account of her proposed book about railway towns, a sample chapter, three possible titles. She had titled the document The Train That Changed Everything, which struck her as bold when she was calm and faintly ridiculous when she was tired.

The weather thickened as they crossed the border. Water crawled in silver threads down the glass. The conductor passed through the carriage twice, first with a clipped apology about delays, then with the sort of shrug that placed responsibility somewhere between the clouds and the railway administration. Isabel checked the connection. Fourteen minutes had become nine, then six.

She packed before the station appeared. Laptop away; notebook into the outside pocket; phone charger wrapped around her hand. The actions were familiar enough to quiet her. Across the aisle, an elderly woman folded a knitted scarf with care, though she had nowhere to put it. A student leaned over his screen, listening to music loud enough for the drums to be heard above the rain.

Rosenstadt arrived in a blaze of reflected light. The train eased beneath the iron roof, where lamps glowed against smoke-darkened glass. Isabel was already standing when it stopped. Outside, the platform was crowded with people holding bags over their heads, coats clinging to their shoulders, faces turned towards the departure boards. Somewhere a bell rang; somewhere else a speaker began to speak and was swallowed by the high, wet echo of the station.
She stepped down, found the connecting board, and saw the words that had not been in her plan: WESTBOUND NIGHT TRAIN — DEPARTED.

For a moment she read them as if they were a mistake in a language she understood perfectly. Then the board changed to its next announcement, leaving her with the wet platform, the case at her feet, and a blue-ink itinerary that had ceased to describe anything.
She checked the time, though the time had not caused the train to leave. 20.11. The next westbound service was at 06.37.

At the information desk a queue curved around a pillar painted with faded red arrows. People stood close enough to share the same rain. A man in a shiny leather jacket spoke into his phone with the careful loudness of someone who wished the whole station to know he had been wronged. A woman held a sleeping toddler beneath her coat. Isabel joined the line and opened the railway app.

Her battery was at eleven per cent. The app offered a replacement route with two changes, the first of them at a station she could not pronounce and the second marked ‘subject to disruption’. She took a screenshot. The screen dimmed before it saved.

At the front of the queue, a woman in a dark uniform was explaining something to a young couple. She had short brown hair tucked behind one ear and a narrow strip of silver at the temples. Her badge said M. KOVÁCS. She listened to their question without interrupting, then pointed to a map with a blunt finger.
‘The hotel bus does not stop there,’ she said. ‘It stops on the other side of the square. If you get on the airport bus, you will have a longer evening than you planned.’

The couple thanked her and moved away. Isabel watched the woman’s face settle into impatience as the next passenger approached. It seemed to her that the woman had decided in advance how much trouble each person was permitted to be.

When Isabel reached the desk, she laid out her problem in its most manageable form: missed connection, ticket details, meeting in the morning. She did not mention Adrian, the rejected proposal, or the fact that the phrase ‘next morning’ had begun to feel less like a delay than an accusation.
Marta checked the ticket and tapped at the keyboard. ‘The train left on time from here.’
‘It arrived late from Brno.’
‘Yes. I can see that.’ Marta spoke without warmth, but not without attention. ‘Your ticket is valid on the morning service. There’s no earlier train. The bus routes are also affected by the storm.’
‘Is there somewhere I can wait?’
‘There are benches.’ Marta looked up. ‘You’re asking whether there’s a bed.’
Isabel heard the impatience and mistook it for indifference. ‘I suppose I am.’

‘Then you need a room. The station hotel is full. There are others across the river, but you should telephone before walking anywhere.’ Marta turned a small card towards her, listing two numbers in careful handwriting. ‘And charge your phone before you leave. The sockets on this side are broken.’
It was helpful advice delivered as though Isabel had made a foolish request. She took the card. ‘Thank you.’

‘The first number may not answer. The second is a bakery that stays open late. They have a public telephone, though I don’t know if the line works in this weather.’ Marta had already reached for the next person’s ticket. ‘It worked yesterday.’

Isabel stepped aside. She now had three per cent battery, one hotel number, and a bakery telephone that might or might not work. The meeting remained at nine. Her blue-ink plan, folded in her notebook, was becoming something she carried rather than something she followed.
She went towards the station doors. Beyond the glass, the square shone beneath the storm. The river was somewhere in the darkness, and across it lay a room she had not yet found.

chapters.title: The Counter
pages: The station doors resisted the wind, then opened with a suddenness that pushed Isabel’s coat against her legs. Rosenstadt’s square spread out in wet black stone. Tram rails ran through it like parallel pencil marks, vanishing beneath the rain. On the opposite side, a line of night buses waited with their interior lights on, their windows fogged by passengers and breath.

She stopped beneath the awning and called the first hotel. A recorded voice answered in German, then in English, with apologies that sounded less personal than the weather. The second number rang until it clicked off. At the third attempt her phone warned that it had entered low-power mode.

A bus moved away from the kerb. Its destination display said RIVER DISTRICT. Isabel had seen the words on the map, though not the route. She could walk, but Marta’s advice had been plain, and the pavement sloped towards a dark avenue. She resented needing to obey a stranger more than she resented the advice itself.

The bakery was two streets from the station, marked by a pale awning and a small brass sign. It had no grand windows or inviting display. Through the glass she saw a counter, a kettle, and three people sitting at separate tables with the serious expressions of those who had missed something. A bell over the door gave a tired ring when she entered.

Warm air met her, carrying the smell of yeast, wet wool and coffee. The floor was tiled in cream and green squares, each one polished by generations of shoes. Behind the counter, a broad-shouldered man was arranging rolls on a tray. He wore a white apron over a striped shirt and had flour on one cheek.
‘You want to call the guesthouse?’ he asked. His English was good, though he said ‘guesthouse’ as if it were a single complicated word.
‘If I can.’
He pointed to a black telephone fixed to the wall near the back. ‘It usually calls.’
‘Usually?’
‘Tonight the weather is having opinions.’ He considered her expression. ‘It is free. Try.’

Isabel dialled the number Marta had written. The line rang, crackled, and rang again. On the fifth ring a woman answered. Isabel gave her name and asked about a room. There was a pause, a question in the background, then the woman said she was sorry: a pipe had broken on the top floor and the last room was not available.
‘I understand,’ Isabel said. She almost laughed at the phrase. ‘Could you recommend somewhere else?’
The woman supplied a hotel name and an address, speaking slowly enough for Isabel to write it down. It was on the far side of the river. She thanked her and hung up.
The baker placed a cup of coffee on the counter without asking. ‘You look like you need one.’
‘That obvious?’
‘No. But the coffee is ready.’ He gave the cup a small push towards her. ‘It costs less than taking a taxi and more than regretting it.’
The coffee was strong and bitter, with a thin skin forming at the edge. Isabel drank it standing up. The warmth reached her hands first. For a few minutes she could think in complete sentences.

Her phone showed one per cent. She found an email address for the hotel and began typing a reservation request. The screen went black before she had finished the word ‘arrival’. She pressed the button, waited, pressed it again. Nothing.
The baker watched her. ‘No charge?’
‘No battery.’
He gestured towards a socket beneath a shelf. ‘You can use that. But the plug is loose. Don’t touch it while the kettle is on.’

She had a charger, but not the correct adapter. The small plastic converter she kept in her case had worked in every other country. Here it sat uselessly beside the socket, its prongs refusing to enter. She tried once, then again, then put it away.
‘There’s a place across the square,’ the baker said. ‘They hire rooms above a bar. Not beautiful.’
‘Clean?’
‘That is a different question.’ He shrugged. ‘Call first.’
He found her a local directory, the pages swollen at the edges, and turned to the Hs. Isabel copied down a number. The telephone still worked, at least in the limited sense that it produced a tone.

A woman answered on the fourth ring. There was one room, she said, but she could not promise it would be quiet. Isabel booked it before she could ask what quiet meant. The address was on the square, near the bus stop. For the first time that evening, something had gone according to a plan, though it was not the plan she had made.
She paid for the coffee. The baker pushed a paper bag across the counter as well.
‘A roll,’ he said. ‘You can pay for it in the morning if you remember.’
‘I can pay now.’
‘Then I will be surprised in the morning.’ He smiled, not unkindly, and turned to the tray. ‘There is no need to make every kindness into an account.’
The remark irritated her because it was close enough to something she might have written. She took the bag anyway.

The storm had not weakened. Isabel crossed the square with one hand holding her hood down and the other gripping the handle of her case. The buses passed in heavy succession, their tyres hissing through puddles. Their lights seemed to slide over the stone without illuminating it.

At the far curb, a night bus opened its doors. The driver waited while an old man climbed aboard. The man stopped to search his pockets, blocking the steps. The driver leaned towards him, speaking too quickly to be kind and too practically to be cruel. At last the old man produced his ticket, and the bus departed without comment.

The room above the bar was reached by a narrow staircase smelling of damp wood and frying onions. A woman in a grey cardigan met Isabel at the top. She had a pencil behind one ear and a small dog asleep in a laundry basket.
‘You are the traveller who called. I am Lenka. The bar will close at midnight, or when the customers agree. Your room is over the courtyard, so the music is less.’
‘And the bed?’
Lenka glanced at her. ‘The bed is not responsible for the music.’

The room contained a brass bed, a wardrobe with one door slightly open, and a window facing the courtyard. The radiator made a series of dry clicks. On the wall hung a framed photograph of Rosenstadt before the river embankment had been built, the water spread wide beneath a white sky.
Isabel paid in cash. Lenka gave her a key with a blue plastic tag and pointed out the bathroom. ‘If the hot water stops, wait five minutes. If it does not return, tell me in the morning.’
‘I have to leave at six.’
‘Then tell me before you leave.’

There was no irony in her voice. She was merely arranging the facts as she found them. Isabel put her case beside the bed and checked the time on her watch. 22.14. The morning train was still possible. The meeting was still possible. She could charge her phone in the hotel lobby, call the publisher, and perhaps make the train from Rosenstadt rather than the connection she had missed.

She unfolded the itinerary and laid it on the bedside table. Its precise lines appeared oddly theatrical in the weak yellow light. She had planned the journey as if a good arrangement could protect her from the things that had already happened: Adrian leaving, the proposal being declined, the storm arriving on an ordinary afternoon.

Outside, the river moved unseen beneath the bridge. The buses continued through the square, taking people towards homes Isabel could not identify. She took the roll from the paper bag and ate it standing beside the window. It was warm in the middle and slightly too salty.
In the courtyard below, rain fell from the eaves into a metal bucket. Each drop struck with a small, regular sound, like a clock that had never learned to tell the time.

chapters.title: The Room Above the Bar
pages: At 23.06 the bar below Isabel’s room was still open. Its customers had settled into the stubborn calm of people who had nowhere better to be. A woman sang with the radio, missing most of the notes but none of the feeling. Someone laughed, then coughed. The music travelled through the floorboards in low, uneven pulses.

Isabel sat on the bed with her laptop open, though there was no internet. She had written the beginning of a message to the publisher in her notes: I am sorry, but the delay means—. She deleted it. A later train might still get her there by noon. The meeting could be moved. She could ask. Asking, she reflected, was easier when the request concerned a timetable.

She needed to use the telephone downstairs. The barwoman had said it was available, but Isabel could not remember whether she had meant the telephone near the till or the one in the hallway. She went down carefully, carrying her notebook as though it made her look less like a guest without a phone.
The barwoman, whose name was Lenka’s sister Hana, was polishing glasses. Her hair was pinned up with a pencil. The music had changed to a slow brass tune.
‘The telephone is behind the counter,’ Hana said. ‘It only makes local calls.’
Isabel placed the publisher’s number beside the register. ‘I think this is not local.’
‘Then it won’t work.’ Hana returned to the glasses. ‘You can try. It enjoys disappointing people.’
Isabel dialled. The line gave a brief, hopeful hum, then went dead.
‘Well,’ Hana said. ‘It enjoyed it.’
Isabel laughed despite herself. It was the first sound she had made that did not contain an apology. Hana looked at her over the rim of a glass.
‘You missed a train?’
‘A connection.’
‘Worse. You have already spent the first part of the journey.’
‘I thought missing a train was missing a train.’
‘Not if you paid for the one before it.’ Hana set the glass down. ‘The people who miss the first train are angry with themselves. The people who miss the connection are angry with several countries.’
There was an easy joke in it, but Hana had the expression of someone who had spent years listening to both sorts of anger. Isabel asked if she had lived in Rosenstadt all her life.

‘Since I was twelve. Before that, I lived in a smaller town where nothing arrived late because nothing arrived.’ She began stacking the glasses. ‘My brother says I should move to Vienna. He says the bar is not a future.’
‘Do you want to move?’
‘I want to know what happens if I do.’ Hana paused, then shrugged. ‘That is not the same thing.’

Isabel recognised the distinction and disliked how neatly it fitted into the silence. She thought of Adrian’s last message, which had ended with a question she had not answered: Do you actually want a life with me, or do you just want to know that one is available?

She had read it on a platform in Graz and waited until the train had left before replying. By then she had sent him a paragraph about work, schedules and the next visit. He had said he was tired of being fitted into the spaces left by everything else.
‘The river road is flooded,’ Hana said, interrupting her thoughts. ‘If you are walking to the station in the morning, take the upper street.’
‘I was told there would be a night bus.’
‘There is. It may come.’ Hana glanced at the clock. ‘This is not a criticism of the buses. They are carrying a lot of water tonight.’

A short burst of static came from a small radio near the till. Hana turned it up. A man’s voice gave a weather warning in German. Hana translated only the useful part: the lower bridge was closed to traffic, and the tram service had stopped. The upper bridge remained open to pedestrians, though people were being advised to avoid it unless necessary.
‘The station is across the river,’ Isabel said.
‘Yes.’ Hana dried her hands on her apron. ‘In the morning, we will know more.’
In the morning had become the city’s answer to everything, but for once it sounded less like a refusal than a modest agreement to continue.

Isabel went upstairs. The room had warmed by a few degrees, and the radiator now clicked with a quieter, more settled rhythm. She placed the laptop on the desk and looked at the list of things she could not do: charge the phone, call the publisher, recover the missed train. Beneath it she wrote the things she could do: sleep, ask about the bridge, try the station again.

The list was so plain that she felt ashamed of it. She had made her living describing other people’s journeys as though difficulty gave them shape. In her articles, a missed train became a lesson about patience; an unfamiliar city offered itself as a page waiting to be read. She knew how this worked. She also knew that a person caught in the rain did not always want a lesson.
At 00.17 the music stopped. A chair scraped across the floor. Someone shut a door too hard, and the silence that followed seemed borrowed rather than earned.

She undressed, set her alarm for 05.45 and placed the watch beside the bed. Her phone lay black on the desk. She imagined the morning in its most favourable form: a working socket in the station, a train leaving at 06.37, a seat beside a window, a late arrival followed by an apologetic meeting and an editor with enough sympathy to postpone judgement.
It was not impossible. That was the difficulty. She could not give up hope without first doing the arithmetic.

Sleep came in brief stretches. In one, she stood in the station with her suitcase and watched departure times change as soon as she read them. In another, she was back in London, arranging cups in Adrian’s kitchen because he had said he was coming home late and she had not known what else to do.
At 04.58 she woke to a sound like furniture being dragged over stone. The window rattled. Rain struck the glass in hard, slanting lines. The city seemed to have moved closer in the dark.

She checked her watch. The alarm had not yet rung. She stood by the window and looked down into the courtyard. The bucket beneath the eaves was overflowing. Water ran across the paving towards a narrow drain, carrying a torn receipt with it.
The river remained hidden beyond the roofs. She could hear it now, not as a distinct sound but as a low, continuous pressure beneath the storm.

At 05.45 the alarm rang. Isabel switched it off before the second note. She dressed, folded the itinerary and put it into the outer pocket of her case. The plan still had a use: it reminded her what she had intended, even if it could no longer tell her what to do.
Downstairs, Hana had unlocked the bar and was making coffee. Her eyes were tired, and she wore a thick jumper beneath her apron.
‘The upper bridge?’ Isabel asked.
‘Open for now. I called the station. The road is flooded, but the pedestrian path may be passable. The bus has not come.’
‘You called the station?’
‘My sister did. The telephone here is useless, but hers works.’ Hana poured coffee into a paper cup. ‘Take this. You look less prepared than yesterday.’
Isabel almost said she was prepared. Instead, she took the cup. ‘Thank you.’
‘It is only coffee,’ Hana said, as if protecting the gesture from praise.

Outside, the first grey light had made the wet square look less like a mirror and more like a place people had to cross. Isabel lifted her case. She was still hoping to reach the train. She no longer thought hope was the same as a timetable.

chapters.title: The Upper Bridge
pages: The rain had softened to a steady fall, but the square was already taking on the river’s colour. Isabel followed the upper street past shuttered shops and a tram stop where a printed notice had peeled away from the glass. The city smelled of stone, wet leaves and coal smoke from somewhere beyond the rooftops.

She had expected a bus. Instead, she found two parked at the curb, their doors shut, their destination screens dark. A driver stood beside the first, smoking beneath his cap. When Isabel asked whether it was running to the station, he shook his head.
‘The bridge is closed to buses. We wait for instructions.’
‘How long?’
He pointed his cigarette towards the sky. ‘Instructions come from above.’
It was difficult to tell whether he meant the city office or the weather. Isabel thanked him and continued on foot.

The upper bridge climbed between old stone buildings. At its entrance a police barrier stood across the road, but a narrow path remained open for pedestrians. The river below had risen close to the lower lamps on the quay. It moved fast and brown, carrying branches that spun against one another, then vanished under the bridge.

She stopped. She could see the station beyond the water, its iron roof brightening in the morning. The shortest route was across the bridge. The other route led uphill through streets she did not know. She could perhaps make the train if she crossed now. She might also find that the path had closed by the time she reached its middle.
A cyclist passed her, pushing rather than riding his bicycle. He lifted one shoulder in greeting. An old woman behind him held a folded umbrella over a paper bag of bread. Neither seemed hurried.
Isabel checked her watch. 06.12. Twenty-five minutes until departure.

She was measuring distance against minutes when a familiar uniform came into view. Marta Kovács stood beside the police barrier, speaking to an officer in a dark coat. She held a clipboard under one arm and had a radio clipped to her shoulder. Her hair was damp at the temples.
Marta saw Isabel and lifted her chin. ‘You are going to the station.’
‘I am trying to.’
‘The path is open. The road is closed. If the water rises further, the path will close too.’ She turned towards the officer. ‘We have been told to clear it if it reaches the lower stones.’
Isabel glanced at the river. ‘Is it safe now?’
‘It is open now,’ Marta said. ‘That is not the same answer.’
The distinction landed with more force than it deserved. Isabel looked down at her case. Its wheels had caught grit from the pavement, and one of them made a small, persistent squeak.
Marta noticed. ‘You have time to cross if you do not stop. But do not use the lower steps. Keep to the centre, and if an officer asks you to turn back, you turn back.’
‘And the train?’
‘I don’t know. The service board says it is running. That can change.’
‘You work at the station. Can’t you find out?’

Marta’s expression tightened, not with offence but with fatigue. ‘I can find out what the station knows. I cannot make it know more.’ She checked the radio. ‘The signal staff are checking the west line. There was a report of debris near the river bend.’
There it was: an answer with no comfort in it. Isabel found herself wanting Marta to sound more certain, and understanding that she would have called the certainty dishonest.
‘You seem to know everyone’s problem,’ Isabel said.
‘It is my job to know which ones I can solve.’
‘And the others?’
‘They become the next shift’s job.’ Marta gave a brief, dry smile. ‘Or the passenger’s.’
A crackle came from her radio. She listened, replied in German, then looked across the river. ‘The train is delayed. Not cancelled.’

The time on the board was not yet official, Marta explained, but the departure would not be at 06.37. It might leave in twenty minutes, or an hour. If Isabel needed to reach the station, she could cross the bridge. If she wanted a guarantee, there was none.

The rain tapped against the case. Isabel could see the station doors, the same entrance she had left the night before. Behind them waited the departure board, the queue, and the possibility of trying again.
‘You can leave the case with me,’ Marta said. ‘I am going back to the station.’
It was not a grand offer. She spoke as if proposing the most practical arrangement, and her eyes were already on the river.
Isabel hesitated. ‘You would carry it?’
‘I did not say I would carry it. I said you could leave it in the station office, if you come with me.’

The offer was less convenient than Isabel had first imagined. She would have to walk with Marta, and arrive without her own luggage in the place where she had already failed to manage matters alone. She could refuse and drag the case herself. Neither choice made the train more certain.
‘All right,’ Isabel said.
Marta held out her hand. ‘I’ll take the handle. You keep the notebook. It looks important.’
‘It’s mostly lists.’
‘Then it is important.’

They crossed at the centre of the bridge. Water rushed beneath the paving, loud enough to soften the traffic noise from the far bank. The stone parapet was slick. Isabel held her free hand against it and watched each step. Halfway across, she thought of Adrian’s question again. Do you actually want a life with me, or do you just want to know that one is available?
She had answered that evening with a description of her next assignment. It had been accurate, but accuracy was not the same as an answer.
Marta walked steadily, without looking at the river. At the opposite end she passed the case back.
‘Thank you,’ Isabel said.
‘It is fine.’
‘You don’t have to make it sound as if it was nothing.’
Marta’s hand stayed on the handle for a moment. ‘It was not nothing. It was a bag.’ She released it. ‘People are often grateful for the part that is easiest to name.’
Isabel did not know what to do with that, so she did not turn it into a lesson. She asked whether Marta had been on shift all night.
‘Since ten.’
‘That’s long.’

‘It is the night shift.’ Marta looked towards the station. ‘My son is at home with his father. He will be at school before I get there. We arrange our lives around the rota. It is not very romantic, but it is effective.’
There was no invitation to admire her. Isabel said, ‘I hope he doesn’t mind.’
‘He minds that I miss breakfast. He does not mind the trains.’

Inside the station, the air was heavy with damp coats and coffee. People had gathered around the boards again. A cleaner pushed a wide mop across the entrance, sending a thin wave of water towards the doors. The platform lamps gave the wet floor a polished, almost ceremonial shine.

Marta led Isabel to a staff window. A colleague took her case and stored it behind a locked door. Isabel was given a paper tag. The train was now listed as delayed by forty minutes. The departure time had acquired a question mark on the local board.
She looked at it and felt her hope rise, absurd and stubborn.
Marta glanced at her. ‘It may go.’
‘You say that like it isn’t good news.’
‘It is better than cancelled.’ Marta checked the radio again. ‘It is not the same as leaving.’

Isabel understood that the distinction mattered. She sat on a bench beneath the station clock, holding the paper tag and the remaining warmth of Hana’s coffee. The meeting in the west was still waiting for her, though she could no longer picture the room. For the first time, she wondered what she would say if she arrived.

chapters.title: A Window Facing the Tracks
pages: At 07.04 the board changed from DELAYED to AWAITING INFORMATION. The people beneath it read the words, then looked around as though information might be standing among them. A man in a wool hat began pacing. The mother with the sleeping toddler had found a place on the floor beside a radiator. A student was using a power socket with the concentrated gratitude of someone who had discovered a small country.

Isabel’s meeting was at nine, but the publisher’s office was two hours from the western station. Even if the train left immediately, even if it made no further stops, she would not arrive on time. The arithmetic was finished. Her mind continued to perform it.

She borrowed a charger from the station café. The young woman behind the counter lent it without ceremony, warning Isabel that it was slow and belonged to her brother. The phone came to life at nine per cent. There were four messages: one from the hotel, one from a colleague, two from the publisher.

The publisher’s first message asked whether she had left Rosenstadt. The second said the meeting could be moved to video, but their editor had only until midday. Isabel read it twice. The meeting had not been saved; it had been altered into something possible.
She typed: I’m delayed by the storm and the missed connection. I can join by video if the station has a connection. I understand if that is not useful.
She almost added an apology for the weather. Instead she sent the message as it was.

Marta was speaking with a station manager by the departure board. Isabel watched her point to the printed service report, then to a map on the wall. She was not trying to persuade him that the train should leave. She was asking what information he needed before he could say whether it would.
When she came back, Isabel showed her the publisher’s message. ‘Is there somewhere with internet?’
‘There is a hotel lobby two blocks away. They sometimes let people use the connection if they buy coffee.’
‘Sometimes?’
‘It depends who is working.’
Marta paused, then added, ‘I can ask at the staff office. We have a terminal, but the public network is unreliable. I cannot promise a video call.’
‘You’ve already done a lot.’
‘I have done what I can do.’ Her voice was matter-of-fact. ‘There is a difference.’

Isabel had judged Marta too quickly the night before. The judgement had been convenient: impatience meant indifference, just as a precise itinerary meant competence. She had mistaken a manner for a motive because the distinction took less time.
‘Could you ask?’ Isabel said. ‘I’d be grateful.’

Marta gave a small nod and went through the staff door. She returned ten minutes later with permission for Isabel to use a terminal in the ticket office. The connection was not strong enough for video, but she could send an email and arrange an audio call from the hotel if the network there worked.
It was not a solution. It was a useful next step.

The train remained delayed. The station manager announced that there was debris near the western line and that engineers were inspecting the track. He did not say when they would finish. The notice was followed by a second announcement in three languages, each one calm enough to make the waiting feel official.

Isabel sent a short email to the publisher. She described what had happened and asked to reschedule the conversation for later that morning. She did not explain how important the commission was to her, or how much she had wanted to return with a good story of the journey. She had not yet earned the right to call it a story.
When she came back to the hall, Marta was drinking coffee from a paper cup. ‘You can stay here,’ she said. ‘Or find somewhere warmer. If the line opens, they will announce it.’
‘Do you know when your shift ends?’
‘At eight.’
‘And then you go home?’
‘If the buses are running.’ Marta looked at the black station windows. ‘My son will be pleased I am late. He likes breakfast with his father.’
Isabel smiled. ‘That’s good, isn’t it?’
‘It is convenient.’ Marta’s mouth curved slightly. ‘Good is a larger word.’

They stood together beneath the board. The delay had already taken Isabel beyond the morning she had planned, but it had not yet taken the day. That thought was not brave or profound. It was simply new.

At 07.51 the service was suspended until further notice. A groan moved through the hall, mild but collective. People began to call relatives, employers, hotels. Isabel’s phone was at twelve per cent. The question mark beside the train number disappeared; the line was now blank.

She could return to the room above the bar, but Hana had warned that the upper bridge might close. She could book a hotel nearer the station and wait. She could continue west by road, if the roads were open. None of the options restored the morning she had lost.

Marta came back from the staff office with her coat on. The shift had ended. ‘There is a taxi stand at the south entrance. The drivers are taking passengers to the river district, not across the closed road. You can ask there.’
‘Would you come with me?’
The question escaped before Isabel had made it sound independent. She waited for the familiar impulse to soften it with an excuse. She let it stand.
Marta studied her for a moment. ‘I’m going home in the other direction.’
‘Right. Sorry.’
‘I can walk you to the entrance. That is not the same thing.’ She lifted her bag from the staff room. ‘And I have to stop at the bakery. My son wants rolls for his class.’

They crossed the hall together. Behind them, the boards changed again, the blank line replaced by a notice that engineers would provide an update at 09.00. No one knew whether the update would contain good news.

The rain had eased to mist. The square smelled of wet stone and diesel, with the first warm scent of bread reaching out from the bakery on the corner. Night buses moved slowly through the streets, their windows clouded, carrying tired passengers towards ordinary morning obligations. On the river, the water remained high. It had taken a branch, a plastic crate and the reflection of the bridge, but no one could say where they had gone.
At the bakery, the baker was placing rows of dark rolls in the window. He recognised Isabel and nodded towards the paper bag in her hand.
‘You remembered to pay?’
‘I paid last night.’
‘Then I am disappointed. I thought I had done you a favour.’

Marta bought six rolls. She spoke to the baker in Hungarian, and he wrapped them in brown paper. They exchanged a few practical remarks about the station and the bridge. Isabel understood none of the words but recognised the ease of two people who had shared enough weather to stop discussing it as an event.
Outside, Marta checked the route on a folded map. ‘There is a small hotel near the upper tram stop. I cannot tell you whether it has rooms. The river road is closed, so take the hill street.’

‘Thank you.’ Isabel wanted to add that she had been wrong about her, but the confession seemed to ask Marta for a response she had not offered. She said instead, ‘You were right about the phone. I should have charged it before leaving the station.’
‘Yes,’ Marta said. ‘You should.’
They both laughed. It was a small sound, but it belonged to them rather than to the weather.
At the fork in the street, Marta turned towards the east side of the city. Her coat was damp at the shoulders; the paper bag of rolls was tucked beneath her arm.
‘I hope you reach your meeting,’ she said.
‘So do I.’
‘That is not much of a plan.’
‘It’s what I have.’
Marta considered this, then nodded. ‘Sometimes that is the useful part.’

She left without waiting to see what Isabel would do next. Isabel stood for a moment with her case, the station ticket still folded in her pocket, and the morning spread ahead of her without a timetable she trusted.

Then she took the uphill street towards the hotel. She would ask whether they had a room. She would ask for a socket, and a local call, and, if necessary, help with the route west. The words did not make her less independent. They only gave independence somewhere to begin.

chapters.title: The Last Table
pages: By the time Isabel left the hotel, the rain had altered its character. It no longer fell in separate drops but travelled sideways, joining the gutters in shining ropes. She had spent twenty minutes at the window facing the tracks, watching the signal lights appear and disappear behind the weather. Her phone, newly charged but stubbornly slow to wake, showed no useful change: the onward train she had missed remained missed, and the morning connection she had hoped to salvage was marked as uncertain. The timetable in blue ink, folded in her coat pocket, had begun to soften at the creases.

At reception, the night clerk had recommended the historic centre as somewhere to wait, though he had admitted that most places would be shut. Isabel could have stayed in her room. Instead, she told herself she needed food, and then corrected herself: she needed to stop staring at the clock. These were not quite the same thing.

She crossed beneath the station arcade and followed a street that descended towards the river. Rosenstadt's old buildings leaned towards one another across the narrow lanes, their upper floors dark, their lower stones polished by centuries of feet and several hours of rain. The paving was uneven. Isabel walked carefully, not because she feared falling, she told herself, but because her shoes had smooth soles.

A night bus groaned past, nearly empty except for a man asleep against the window. Its yellow interior moved through the rain like a small room being carried away. At the next junction, Isabel paused beneath a carved stone angel whose face had been worn almost blank. She could see, two streets ahead, a café still lit. Its sign, painted with a black cup and a gold star, swung in the wind.

The café was called Weber's. Inside, chairs stood upside down on half the tables, and a young man in a white shirt was wiping the counter with the discouraged attention of someone who had already done it once. He looked up as Isabel entered.
‘We’re closing,’ he said, without unkindness. ‘Unless you have a convincing reason.’
‘I have a wet coat and a phone with six per cent battery.’
He considered this. ‘The phone is the more persuasive of the two. The coat seems to have made its own arrangements.’

His name, she discovered, was Lukas Weber. He let her plug her phone beside the till and put a cup of coffee in front of her, though he warned her the machine had been cleaned. It tasted faintly of burnt hazelnuts and was warmer than the room had any right to be. He found bread, sliced cheese and a jar of apricot preserve in the kitchen.
‘It isn’t a menu,’ he said. ‘It’s what survived the day.’
‘That sounds familiar.’
‘To the bread or to you?’

She smiled, and for a moment felt the effort of it. Outside, water ran down the window in crooked lines. Lukas turned the sign to CLOSED, then remained on his side of the counter rather than hurrying her.

Isabel explained about the missed connection, the wasted hours, and the uncertain morning train. She kept her account neat, as if giving it in the right order might make it less irritating. Lukas listened, then said, ‘Trains are very good at making lateness look like a personal failure.’
‘I had a plan.’
‘Most people do. The railway has plans too. They don’t always speak to each other.’ He said it lightly, but when she asked whether he had always worked in the café, his hand paused over the cloth.
‘No,’ he said. ‘I was training as an architect in Brno. I had a place at a studio there. Then my father’s health got worse, and my sister couldn’t manage everything alone.’

He added that his father had since died, his sister had moved to Prague, and he had never quite returned to architecture. The café, he said, had started as a temporary arrangement. He did not claim the choice had made him wiser or happier. Some days it seemed generous; some days it seemed like a door he had closed himself.
‘People prefer a clean story,’ Lukas said, stacking cups. ‘The sort where you give something up and are rewarded with meaning. Real life is less tidy. I’m still not sure what I gave up, exactly.’

Isabel looked down at her coffee. She had spent years regarding her independence as proof that nobody could inconvenience her. Lately it had begun to resemble a habit of never allowing anyone close enough to try.
Her phone lit at last. A message from Nadia appeared: ‘Still at station. They’re asking me to pay extra to keep case overnight. Do you know anywhere cheap?’
Lukas read the worry in her face before she showed him the screen. ‘A friend?’
‘Someone I met today.’
‘Then ask someone who knows the city,’ he said. ‘That is what cities are for, when the maps stop helping.’

chapters.title: A Question at Closing Time
pages: Nadia called rather than reply. Her voice arrived through Isabel’s phone with a thin, metallic edge, and behind it came the station’s public-address system, announcing a platform change for a train that had already departed.
‘I’m at the lockers,’ Nadia said. ‘They won’t take my card, and I’m not leaving the instrument case in the waiting room.’
‘What instrument?’

‘Viola. It’s not a cello, though people keep asking.’ There was a rustle, then a sigh. ‘I have a room booked for tonight, technically, but it’s across town and they want cash for the deposit. I thought the tour manager had paid. He thought I had. We’re both very organised.’
Isabel glanced at Lukas. He was taking a stack of saucers into the kitchen, but the door remained open.
‘Could you come to Weber’s?’ Isabel asked. ‘It’s closed, but I’m here.’
‘Is that safe?’
‘It’s a café, not a tunnel.’
‘I meant for you.’

The concern in Nadia’s voice was practical, not intimate, and Isabel found she preferred it that way. She gave her the street name and a description of the gold-star sign. Lukas, when she explained, shrugged as if a musician with a large case was no more extraordinary than a delivery of milk.
‘I can stay until she gets here,’ he said. ‘After that, I’m going to the hospital.’

He said this as he put on a dark jacket. His father had not been there, Isabel realised; Lukas was speaking of someone else. He explained that his neighbour, Mr Havel, had fallen at home and been taken in earlier. Lukas had promised to bring his glasses and a clean shirt. The neighbour’s daughter was on a coach from Linz, delayed by the storm.
‘You visit him often?’ Isabel asked.
‘Often enough to know he’ll complain about the shirt.’ Lukas locked the till. ‘He prefers the old one. It has a stain shaped like Italy.’

Nadia came in twelve minutes later, carrying her viola case with one hand and a canvas bag with the other. She was twenty-four, though the way she studied a room made her seem younger, and the way she negotiated with Lukas about borrowing his phone charger made her seem older. Her hair was damp at the ends. She set the case down carefully, checked both latches, and only then took off her coat.
‘Sorry,’ she said. ‘The bus stopped twice, and the second time nobody knew why.’
‘That’s the city’s way of welcoming you,’ Lukas said. ‘It wants you to practise patience.’
‘I’m already a musician. I have enough patience.’ Nadia looked at the covered chairs and then at the plate Lukas had left out. ‘Is that for sale?’
‘It is what survived the day,’ Isabel said.
Nadia gave a short laugh. ‘Then it should be expensive.’

She explained that the tour had been arranged by a small ensemble playing in towns along the river. The first concert had gone well; the second had been cancelled when their pianist became ill. Her manager had asked everyone to remain available, but had not sent money for extra accommodation. Nadia could return to her family in Olomouc, if she abandoned the remaining dates, or continue with the tour and hope the organiser paid what was owed.
‘I can’t afford to be noble,’ she said. ‘I also can’t afford to go home and tell my teacher I left after one cancelled concert.’
‘Those aren’t your only choices,’ Isabel said, too quickly.
Nadia’s eyes lifted. ‘You have a third one?’

‘No. I’m only saying—’ Isabel stopped. She had meant to offer a solution, but what she had was a polished objection. She knew how useless it could be to hear that a problem had many possible answers from someone who had not yet paid the bill.

Lukas wrote down the address of a modest guesthouse near the bus depot. The owner sometimes let musicians pay part in the morning, he said, but he could not promise anything. He also gave them the number of the night-bus information line and marked which route stopped near the hospital.
‘Why the hospital?’ Isabel asked.
‘Because I’m going there.’ He placed Mr Havel’s glasses in his pocket. ‘And the bus is the same one you’d take to the guesthouse. It isn’t an offer to solve your evening, just a direction.’
Nadia read the address twice. ‘I can ask them. I don’t need to pretend I have money I don’t have.’
‘Good,’ Lukas said. ‘The pretending is usually more tiring.’

He held the door while they stepped into the rain. Isabel noticed that he did not tell them to be brave or to trust the city. He simply waited until both had their coats fastened, then set off towards the bus stop with the glasses in his pocket.

chapters.title: The Bus Along the River
pages: The night bus came with its interior lights dimmed and its windows clouded by the warmth of other passengers. Lukas climbed aboard first, and Nadia followed, manoeuvring the viola case between the seats. Isabel came last. There were only six people on the bus: a woman in a supermarket uniform, two students sharing earphones, a man asleep with his head against the glass, and a boy holding a paper bag that leaked water onto his shoes.

The bus pulled away from the kerb. Rosenstadt slid by in fragments: shuttered shops, a pharmacy cross glowing green, the yellow windows of an apartment block where somebody was still awake. At the river, the road bent sharply. The water below was black except where streetlamps broke across it in long, trembling bars.
Nadia sat with the case upright between her knees. ‘If I leave it on its side, the bridge might get the wrong idea,’ she said.
‘What idea?’ Isabel asked.
‘That it can throw us into the river.’
She said it dryly, then turned her attention to her phone. Her tour manager had sent a message: Can you cover tonight? I’ll sort reimbursement tomorrow. Nadia read it twice and put the phone away.
‘He may mean it,’ Isabel said.
‘He may. But I’ve covered three costs already, and “tomorrow” is a word that travels light.’

There was no bitterness in this, only arithmetic. Isabel recognised it. She had made her own decisions by the same method, though she had disguised them as principle. She wanted to ask Nadia why she stayed on the tour if the terms were so poor, but could hear how easily the question might become a judgement.

The bus stopped opposite the hospital. Lukas lifted the viola case down the step and set it on the pavement without touching the strings. Nadia thanked him. He gave her the guesthouse address again and showed her the correct stop for the return route.
‘I’ll be fine,’ she said.
‘I didn’t ask you to be,’ Lukas replied. ‘I asked whether you knew where you were going.’

The hospital entrance was bright enough to turn every raindrop on the pavement silver. A porter pushed a wheelchair through the automatic doors. Inside, the air smelled of wet wool, floor polish and something faintly medicinal. Lukas checked at reception before Isabel and Nadia followed him to a row of chairs beside the lifts.
‘You don’t have to come in,’ he said.
‘We’re waiting for the bus,’ Nadia answered, though the stop was plainly visible through the windows.

Lukas did not challenge the explanation. He went to the ward desk with Mr Havel’s glasses and the clean shirt. When he returned, he said the neighbour was awake, cross about the food, and unwilling to admit that he had been frightened.
‘So, normal,’ Nadia said.
‘Almost reassuringly.’ Lukas looked towards the corridor. ‘I’ll stay ten minutes. His daughter may arrive later, but the ward has enough people for the practical part.’
‘And the other part?’ Isabel asked.
‘There’s no useful way to measure it.’ He gave a small shrug, as if to keep the sentence from becoming more important than it was. ‘I’m not doing anything remarkable.’
He went back down the corridor. Nadia sat, resting one hand on her case. Isabel remained standing for a while, then sat beside her.
‘I used to think needing someone was the same as failing to manage,’ Isabel said. She had not planned to say this. The words sounded more awkward aloud than they had in her head.
‘That sounds exhausting.’
‘It was efficient.’
‘Those aren’t opposites.’ Nadia adjusted the strap on her canvas bag. ‘I’m good at managing. I’m also very good at not asking until there’s no point.’
Neither of them tried to turn the admission into comfort. The hospital clock moved with its ordinary, indifferent tick. Outside, the river continued to carry the rain towards the dark edge of town.
Nadia checked the guesthouse number. ‘I’ll call before we get on the bus. If they say no, I’ll ask the station hostel. If they say no, I’ll decide then. Not now, when I’m cold and tired.’
‘That’s sensible.’
‘It’s only sensible if it works.’
‘No,’ Isabel said. ‘I think it can be sensible even if it doesn’t.’
The sentence surprised her. It did not sound like a rule she had learned; it sounded like something she had noticed.
When Lukas returned, his hands were empty. ‘He says the shirt is too clean,’ he told them. ‘Apparently it makes the hospital look careless.’
Nadia smiled. ‘You should have left Italy on it.’

‘I’ll remember next time.’ He checked the time on the wall clock and pointed out that their bus was due in four minutes. ‘The guesthouse door will be locked, so ring the bell. Don’t expect poetry from the night porter.’
‘I never do,’ Nadia said.

At the stop, the three of them stood under the shelter while rain drummed on its thin roof. Lukas would take the bus back towards his café. Nadia and Isabel would continue to the guesthouse. No one had been rescued; there were merely addresses, a charged phone, and a plan small enough to revise.

chapters.title: The Guesthouse Bell
pages: The guesthouse stood behind a bakery whose windows were dark and fogged from within. Its sign, a blue enamel plate with one corner missing, announced ROSE COURT in peeling letters. Nadia rang the bell. For a time there was only the rain and, from somewhere inside, the distant clatter of a television. Then an upstairs light came on.
A woman opened the door wearing a wool cardigan over her nightdress. She looked first at the viola case, then at the two women, then at the clock on the wall behind them.
‘We have no double room,’ she said.

Nadia explained the booking she had expected, the cancelled concert and the tour organiser’s confusion. She did not apologise for the facts, only for having arrived so late. The woman listened without interrupting.
‘I can offer you a single room,’ she said at last. ‘Cash in the morning. But there is only one bed, and the building has rules about guests.’
‘We’ll take it,’ Nadia said, then looked at Isabel. ‘If you want to.’

The offer was not generous enough to be a kindness and not difficult enough to be a threat. Isabel considered the hour, the wet streets, and the slight embarrassment of being asked to share a room with someone she had known for less than a day. She considered, too, the old reflex that would have sent her walking elsewhere simply to avoid owing anyone anything.
‘Yes,’ she said. ‘Thank you.’

The guesthouse owner, whose name was Mrs Vlk, told them not to mistake acceptance for a permanent arrangement. The room was hers again at ten. She had laundry to do and no interest in becoming responsible for a travelling musician’s instrument. Nadia assured her that the viola would be kept safely. Mrs Vlk gave her a look that suggested this assurance had been heard before.

The room was narrow, with one bed, a washbasin and a wardrobe that could not quite close. From its window, the station roofs showed in the rain. Nadia laid the viola case across two chairs and tested each latch. Isabel hung their coats on separate pegs.
‘I can take the floor,’ Isabel said.
‘There’s no floor space once the case is there.’ Nadia pulled the blanket straight. ‘We can both sleep in the bed. It’s wide enough, and neither of us has to make this into a moral drama.’
The mattress was indeed wide enough. Nadia placed a rolled-up scarf between them, not as a boundary but as a joke she did not explain. They sat on opposite sides to remove their shoes.
The rain tapped the sill. Downstairs, Mrs Vlk turned off the television. Somewhere outside, a bus released its brakes with a long sigh.

Nadia’s phone rang. She answered in a low voice, listening more than speaking. Her manager’s explanation involved an unpaid invoice, an illness, and a promise to send money when his bank opened. Nadia asked for a specific amount and a specific time. The answer remained vague. She said she would decide in the morning, thanked him for calling, and ended the conversation.
‘Are you going to leave the tour?’ Isabel asked.

‘I don’t know. If I leave, it won’t be because I’m too proud to ask for what I’m owed. If I stay, it won’t be because I’m afraid to disappoint him.’ Nadia put the phone under her pillow. ‘I need to see what the morning looks like.’

Isabel thought of her own timetable, all its narrow boxes and confident arrows. She had believed that if she planned carefully enough, no decision would need to be made in uncertainty. The rain had not destroyed the plan; it had simply exposed how much of it depended on other people, other trains, other choices.
‘I missed a train today,’ she said.
‘You told me.’
‘I keep thinking that if I had moved faster at the platform—’
‘Would the train have waited?’
‘No.’
‘Then you don’t have to keep moving after it.’
Nadia spoke without looking at her, as though she were discussing a practical matter rather than offering comfort. Isabel appreciated that. She turned off the bedside lamp.

Sleep did not come at once. The room held the damp smell of their coats and the warmer smell of old wood. Isabel could hear Nadia breathing lightly, awake beside her. She wanted to ask whether the tour mattered more than the money, whether music could justify such uncertainty, whether Nadia had ever felt foolish for staying. She did not ask. The questions belonged to a morning that had not yet arrived.

Eventually the city’s sounds became less distinct. The river was beyond the buildings, though Isabel could not see it. She imagined it passing under the bridge, carrying reflections that would not stay in one place. The idea was not comforting, exactly. It was simply true.

At some hour, the rain eased. A delivery van moved along the street, and the bakery’s rear door opened. Warm air carried a smell of yeast and toasted flour into the guesthouse stairwell. Isabel woke, heard Nadia shift, and knew dawn was near, though neither of them had slept enough to greet it properly.

chapters.title: The Bread Before Morning
pages: The bakery opened while the sky was still grey. Mrs Vlk knocked once, then told them through the door that she would be locking up at ten, as promised. Nadia had already dressed. Isabel folded the blanket and found the scarf between them, fallen to the floor like a discarded line on a map.

They carried the viola downstairs. The guesthouse owner inspected the case and the room key, then accepted Nadia’s payment in cash from a small purse. There was no argument, only the awkwardness of completing an arrangement that had been made at an hour when both parties were tired.

Outside, the pavement still shone. The storm had left pools along the kerb, but the rain had become a fine mist. At the bakery, a woman in a flour-dusted apron was lifting trays from an oven. The warm smell of bread entered the street before the door opened.
Nadia bought two rolls and a small pastry. ‘I’m not pretending breakfast is a plan,’ she said. ‘It’s breakfast.’

They ate standing beneath the bakery’s striped awning. Across the road, a night bus turned towards the station, its windows bright with the last passengers of the dark. Isabel thought of the people moving through the city at different speeds, each with a destination that might change while they travelled.

Nadia had received a message from her manager. The payment would be sent by midday, he wrote, and the remaining concerts were still possible if she could reach the next town by afternoon. She read the message, then put the phone away.
‘I’ll go to the station and ask whether there’s a cheap train. If the money arrives, I’ll continue. If it doesn’t, I’ll go home. I can explain that to my teacher.’
‘And if he’s disappointed?’
‘Then he’ll be disappointed.’ Nadia took a bite of her roll. ‘I can’t play the viola for his opinion.’

They walked towards the river, keeping to the wider streets where the paving stones were less slippery. The water had risen overnight, brown and flecked with scraps of leaves. On the bridge, a municipal worker in a fluorescent jacket was clearing branches from the railings. He nodded to them without pausing.

Isabel looked back at the station roofs. The trains beyond them would begin to gather their morning crowds: commuters with dry umbrellas, students carrying coffee, people who knew exactly which platform to take. She had once thought such certainty could be acquired by studying a timetable closely enough. Now she understood that knowledge and control were not the same thing.
‘Are you all right?’ Nadia asked.
‘I think so.’ Isabel considered the answer. ‘I’m not sure what I’m supposed to do next.’
‘That’s different from not knowing where you are.’
‘Yes.’

The phone in Isabel’s pocket vibrated. A message from the hotel night clerk said that the room would remain available until noon, but the desk could not guarantee a later extension. A practical note, neither an invitation nor a rebuke. She showed Nadia.
‘You can go back there,’ Nadia said. ‘I’ll manage the station.’

The old response—no, I’m fine; I can do it alone—rose with its familiar efficiency. Isabel let it pass. ‘Would you come with me to ask about extending the room? I’m not sure I’ll understand what they can offer, and you’re better at asking direct questions.’
Nadia smiled. ‘That is true.’
‘I’m not asking you to decide for me.’
‘Good. I’m tired.’

They turned towards the hotel, taking the street that led beneath the bridge and past the hospital bus stop. Isabel felt no sudden transformation. She was still tired, still annoyed at the railway, still inclined to make lists in her head. But she was walking with someone rather than proving that she could walk alone.
At the hotel door she stopped to check her phone. There were no messages that could repair the missed connection or explain the night into a lesson. She put the device away.
‘Come in?’ she asked Nadia.
‘Only as far as reception. I have a train to price, and a manager to doubt.’
‘That sounds sensible.’
‘It may not work.’
‘I think it can be sensible even if it doesn’t.’
Nadia gave her a sideways look. ‘You said that at the hospital.’
‘I know.’
They entered together. Behind them, Rosenstadt’s river moved under the bridge, carrying the storm away without keeping anything it had reflected.

chapters.title: The Waiting Room Clock
pages: By the time Isabel reached Rosenstadt’s central station, the storm had stopped pretending to pass. Rain drove sideways across the forecourt, and every gust made the glass doors shudder in their frames. The bakery’s paper bag was tucked under her coat, warm no longer but still faintly fragrant. She had taken the last night bus as far as the river and walked the remaining distance, following the station clock above the roofs like a rather stern moon.

Inside, the tiled floor reflected the departure board in broken blue lines. Several services had acquired the same small announcement: delayed. Isabel found the platform for her onward train and checked the time twice, though the second check could not make it earlier. The missed connection remained missed. A railway employee had already explained that the storm had brought a tree down beyond the eastern junction; no replacement service could be promised before morning.

She sat in the waiting room beneath a clock whose hands moved with a confidence the trains had not earned. A man across from her was writing on a folded sheet of paper. He stopped every few lines, crossed something out, then began again on the reverse. His coat was brushed and old, his silver hair carefully parted. Beside him stood a leather case with a repaired handle.
After a while he looked up. ‘You’ve checked the board enough times to know it hasn’t improved.’
‘It might have changed.’

‘That is what I tell myself about this letter.’ He lifted the paper, then put it down again. ‘Thomas Reed. Retired history teacher, which means I have spent forty years correcting other people’s dates and the last thirty getting my own wrong.’

Isabel introduced herself. He said he was waiting for the night train to Brünnfeld, where he hoped to meet a woman he had not seen in thirty years. His tone made the hope sound like an appointment arranged by someone else.

‘Her name is Elise,’ he said. ‘We taught at the same school. We were close, in the way people are when they believe there will always be another summer. Then I accepted a post in England. She thought I had made the decision with her already excluded. I thought she had encouraged me to go.’ He turned the paper over. ‘We each received a sentence from the other and supplied the rest.’
‘And the letter?’ Isabel asked.

‘It has been written and rewritten since Tuesday. I can apologise for leaving. I can’t honestly apologise for leaving, because the job mattered to me. I can say I misunderstood her. I can’t say I know what she meant.’ He gave a small, embarrassed shrug. ‘Retirement gives a man too much time to make a clean ending out of untidy facts.’

The station loudspeaker dissolved another announcement into static. Thomas folded the letter carefully along a line already softened by use. He had not told Isabel whether Elise had agreed to meet him. She did not ask. It was clear enough that the answer, whatever it was, had not settled anything.

When the board flickered, he stood and went to the information desk. The queue had formed around a pillar, and he returned with no more than a printed service notice. Isabel checked the railway operator’s website on her phone, then compared it with the paper board. The overnight train was still listed, but the onward connection at Brünnfeld had been cancelled. A regional service would leave later, if the line reopened.
‘Could you ask whether the desk has a number for the local rail office?’ Thomas said. ‘I’m afraid the website assumes I was born knowing where to tap.’

There was no neat answer at the desk. Isabel asked the clerk to check the regional line directly, and the clerk made a call, then wrote a telephone number on Thomas’s notice. It was a small improvement, not a rescue. Thomas thanked her and studied the number as if it were a difficult date on a classroom blackboard.
‘Why must you reach this meeting?’ he asked, looking at her now. ‘And what do you hope to prove by getting there?’

Isabel began with the practical answer: a ticket, a destination, a plan made before the storm. It sounded inadequate even to her. ‘I had a breakup,’ she said. ‘And a job I wanted went to someone else. I told myself this trip was a fresh start. Perhaps I also wanted to prove I could leave everything behind and arrive somewhere new without needing anyone.’
Thomas did not offer a reply at once. Then he said, ‘That is an ambitious use of a railway.’

The irony was gentle, but it found its mark. Isabel looked at the timetable in her hands. She had planned the journey as if competence could keep disappointment from following her. Around them, sleepers shifted under damp coats; a cleaner pushed water towards a drain. The clock went on being certain.
‘I’m not sure what I’ll say if I do reach my destination,’ she said.

‘Nor am I,’ Thomas replied. He refolded his letter, not as though it were finished but as though it could be carried. Outside, rain blurred the station windows until the city became a field of uncertain lights. Neither of them had been given the answer they wanted. For the moment, they had managed to find the right desk.

chapters.title: A Nurse at Dawn
pages: The waiting room filled and emptied in uneven tides. A family arrived with two sleeping children and a bright red suitcase; a man in a delivery uniform left to telephone someone from the platform; an old couple shared a thermos without speaking. Isabel stayed near Thomas, though neither of them had asked the other to. His letter lay inside the leather case now, as if it needed the same shelter from the weather as he did.

At half past four, a woman came in from the street and paused beneath the clock to wring rain from the cuffs of her jacket. She was in her early thirties, with her dark hair caught in a loose knot and the particular stillness of someone who had spent a shift listening for machines. A canvas bag hung from her shoulder. She bought coffee from the vending machine, tasted it, and gave it a look of mild professional disapproval.
‘Night shift?’ Isabel asked, mostly because the woman’s face seemed to recognise the hour.

‘Finished one,’ she said. ‘The hospital is kinder than this coffee, and it has never claimed otherwise.’ Her name was Anna Weiss, a nurse at Rosenstadt General. She had just come off the surgical ward and was waiting for a bus that would take her across the river.

Thomas offered her the other chair. Anna accepted, then rubbed her palms together for warmth. Their talk began with the delays. She knew the storm had flooded a service road near the hospital, though the river itself was still within its banks. ‘People hear “river” and imagine a dramatic rescue,’ she said. ‘Mostly it means checking the drains and hoping the basement pumps behave.’

She spoke with a briskness that did not disguise her exhaustion. On the ward, she said, visitors often asked for the historic centre and the castle hill, as if the city had been built for their photographs. ‘The people who live here are more interested in whether the bakery opens before six and which bus still runs when the river road is closed.’
‘Does it?’ Isabel asked.

‘Usually. “Usually” is doing a lot of work tonight.’ Anna glanced at the departure board. ‘The night buses share drivers with the day routes. When one gets delayed, everyone knows before the official notice does, because someone’s cousin is waiting at the depot.’

A tired laugh escaped Isabel. She had spent hours treating travel as a private test, but the city kept presenting itself as a network of people whose work continued whether or not a visitor understood it. Anna explained which bus reached the hospital entrance and which stopped nearer the ordinary residential streets beyond it. The useful route depended on where Isabel needed to go, not on what was picturesque.

‘You could walk along the river,’ Anna said. ‘There’s a covered stretch beside the old warehouses. It’s not the route for a photograph, especially in this rain. But it avoids the flooded corner, and you can see where the neighbourhood wakes up.’

Isabel looked at Thomas. He was listening, though his gaze had settled on the leather case between his shoes. His train remained uncertain. Anna had a bus to catch and another day to begin after a few hours’ sleep.
‘Are you travelling alone?’ Anna asked Isabel.
‘Yes.’

‘That wasn’t quite what I asked.’ She said it without challenge, then blew across her coffee. ‘I live alone. I don’t always feel lonely. They’re not opposite conditions, if that’s what you’re wondering.’
Isabel considered the distinction. ‘I think I’ve been trying to make them the same. If I can manage everything alone, then I won’t have to feel the other thing.’

‘That sounds tiring,’ Anna said. She did not decorate the observation with advice. ‘At work, you can be surrounded all night and still be lonely. You can also sit quietly with one person and feel less alone without telling them your whole life.’
Thomas glanced at the clock. ‘A useful arrangement.’
‘Not always,’ Anna said. ‘Sometimes the person talks through the film.’

The joke was small, and it let the seriousness rest. Isabel asked Anna about Rosenstadt beyond the centre. Anna described the workers’ entrance at the hospital, the laundrette that stayed open late, and a row of apartment blocks where the balconies filled with herbs in summer. Her affection for the city was not sentimental. She complained about the rent, the unreliable buses and the council’s habit of repairing paving stones in the wrong order. Then she mentioned the river in winter, when the mist made the opposite bank disappear, and her voice softened.

When the bus announcement finally came, it was for Anna’s route. She stood, slung her bag over her shoulder, and told Isabel which door to use if she went towards the hospital. ‘The main entrance is bright and obvious. The staff entrance is less confusing if you’re meeting someone who works nights.’
‘Thank you,’ Isabel said.
‘You’re welcome. And don’t trust that coffee machine.’ Anna raised the paper cup in farewell and went out into the rain.

The doors closed behind her. Thomas turned his notice over and read the handwritten number again. Isabel watched the empty space Anna had left, aware that being helped had not made her journey less hers. The next bus rumbled somewhere beyond the glass.

chapters.title: The City Before Its Visitors
pages: The first bus that came was not Anna’s. Its destination board glowed through the wet glass, and its driver shook his head when passengers asked about the river route. The second bus arrived twenty minutes later, carrying a handful of people who looked as if they had been awake longer than the city. Isabel asked the driver about the hospital stop. He pointed to the middle doors and said, ‘If the road is open, you’ll see the blue sign.’

Thomas stayed in the station. His train had not been cancelled, only postponed, and he preferred to remain close to the board. ‘I have spent enough years making pupils wait for me to arrive,’ he said. ‘I can manage a little waiting myself.’ He had the railway number in his pocket and promised to call if the service changed. The letter remained in his case.

Isabel took Anna’s suggested route. At first the bus followed streets she recognised from the centre, where stone façades pressed close to one another and shop signs swung in the storm. Then it crossed the river, which was swollen and dark beneath the lamps. The water carried reflections downstream in long, broken streaks. On the embankment, two municipal workers dragged a branch from a blocked drain while rain gathered in their hoods.

The hospital stood beyond a wide junction, lit from within and almost colourless in the wet morning. Isabel saw the main entrance first: automatic doors, a shelter for ambulances, a row of damp bicycles chained to the railings. Further round, a narrower door opened onto the staff car park. She did not go in. Anna had not invited her, and there was no reason to turn a helpful direction into an excuse for intrusion.

Instead, she walked along the river towards the residential streets Anna had described. The covered warehouse passage smelled of stone, old wood and the river’s cold breath. Water ticked steadily from the roof. A man in an orange jacket swept grit away from a doorway; he looked up long enough to nod. In a lit basement, a woman stacked clean laundry into plastic baskets. These were not sights the city had arranged for her.

At a small junction, a night bus stopped with its hazard lights blinking. Its driver spoke through the open door to a cyclist whose chain had slipped. Neither seemed surprised to be discussing mechanical trouble before sunrise. The cyclist thanked him and pushed on, trousers dark with rain. Isabel noticed how often the city’s practical kindness took the form of brief attention: a warning, a direction, a door held open without ceremony.

She passed a bakery with its shutters half raised. The smell of warm yeast and burnt sugar drifted into the street. Inside, a baker in a striped apron was arguing with a supplier over a crate. ‘I ordered rye, not a philosophical question,’ she said, and both of them laughed. Isabel bought a small roll and ate it beneath the awning. It was excellent and slightly too hot; she burnt her tongue and did not mind.

Her phone showed a message from the railway operator. No further information. The meeting she had meant to reach still existed somewhere beyond Rosenstadt, but it had become less like a test with a pass mark and more like a conversation whose first sentence she had not yet found. That change did not make her suddenly calm. She still wanted the train to run. She still resented the storm for interrupting a plan she had taken pride in making.

At the edge of the neighbourhood she found a small square with a closed fountain and benches dark with rain. An apartment window above it opened, and someone shook a cloth over the sill. A radio played faintly, then stopped. No one was waiting for visitors. The morning was being assembled out of ordinary tasks.

Isabel thought of the hotel room she had left behind, the station’s bright clock, and the easy story she had told herself about travelling alone. Independence had seemed clean in that story, like a key turning in a lock. Here it looked more like a set of choices: when to ask, when to continue, when to let another person’s knowledge alter the route.

On her return towards the station, she took a wrong turning and found herself beside the river again. She could have checked the map immediately. Instead, she watched the current for a moment, then asked a man carrying a folded umbrella which way led to the central bridge. He gave her two directions and warned her that one pavement was under repair.
‘I thought that was the quicker way,’ she said.
‘It was yesterday,’ he answered, and continued on.

The station came into view through thinning rain. Isabel arrived with wet shoes, a half-eaten roll and no new certainty about the trains. What she carried was less impressive than a solution, but more useful than the plan she had started with: a clearer picture of the city, and the knowledge that asking had cost her very little.

chapters.title: A Route for Ordinary Hours
pages: Morning reached Rosenstadt without ceremony. It appeared first as a pale strip above the roofs, then as a change in the colour of the station glass. The rain weakened to a fine, persistent mist. Isabel came back through the entrance beside a florist’s kiosk, where buckets of tulips stood in water that had collected on the floor. The seller was wiping each leaf with a cloth, apparently unwilling to let the storm have the last word.

The departure board showed a new time for the Brünnfeld train. Thomas was still in the waiting room, reading his notice. He had called the number, but the line had been engaged. His disappointment was not dramatic; it sat in the angle of his shoulders and the care with which he folded the paper.
‘The train may leave in an hour,’ he said. ‘The connection still may not.’
‘And Elise?’

‘I sent a message from the public phone. It went through, at least. No reply yet.’ He looked at the leather case. ‘Perhaps she is asleep. Perhaps she saw the name and decided she had no wish to begin the day with me.’
Isabel sat opposite him. ‘You could still go, even if the connection fails.’

‘I could. That is the irritating part of uncertainty: it leaves you responsible.’ He gave her a brief smile. ‘I used to tell my pupils that history had been made by people who chose under imperfect conditions. I found it more comforting when the choices belonged to dead people.’

His voice was lightly amused, but the letter had returned to his hand. He opened it and read the first paragraph without moving his lips. Isabel saw that he had written Elise’s name at the top and crossed it out, then written it again in smaller letters. It was not the sign of a man who had reached a conclusion. It was the sign of someone trying to approach one.

The railway desk began serving a longer queue. Isabel joined it to ask whether the morning regional trains had resumed. The clerk, the same one from the night, consulted a screen and explained that the line beyond the eastern junction remained restricted. A replacement bus was being arranged, but there was no reliable departure time. Isabel thanked her and returned with the information, careful not to make it sound like a promise.
Thomas listened. ‘A bus, then.’
‘Possibly.’
‘You’ve learnt to use that word.’
‘I’ve had practice since midnight.’

He tapped the folded letter against his knee. ‘If I do reach her, I want to say that I am sorry she had to guess what I was choosing. Not that I chose the work. She had a right to know before I packed.’
‘That sounds more precise than the letter you showed me.’
‘It is. The letter has too many explanations. Explanations are often apologies wearing a better coat.’ He glanced at her. ‘You may tell me if that is nonsense.’
‘It isn’t nonsense,’ Isabel said. ‘Though I’m not sure a person can separate explanation from apology as neatly as a teacher separates dates.’
‘Retired teacher,’ he corrected. ‘I now separate my socks by whether they are dry.’

The announcement for Isabel’s service came at last: delayed again, departure subject to track clearance. The missed connection still had no replacement.
