For a few seconds, she felt the old reflex return: search the timetable, calculate the alternatives, find a way to make the journey obey. Then she heard the announcement properly. Subject to track clearance. The phrase did not invite negotiation.

She called the person she was meant to meet and left a message explaining the delay. She did not claim she would arrive by a particular hour. She asked whether they could keep the afternoon open and promised to call when she knew more. Listening to her own voice after she hung up, she heard uncertainty without apology. That was new.
Thomas looked up from the letter. ‘Was it difficult?’
‘Less difficult than pretending I know what will happen.’
‘A low bar, perhaps. But still a bar.’

They shared the rest of Isabel’s bakery roll. Thomas tore it unevenly and apologised for the crumbs. He spoke about teaching history in a town where the local museum’s most popular exhibit was a broken printing press. He had once taken students there and spent the entire visit correcting the guide’s dates, then realised that he had not asked a single pupil what interested them. ‘I was right about the dates,’ he said. ‘That has not been much comfort.’

Isabel smiled. There was no moral arranged at the end of his story, only the awkward fact that he had noticed something late and could no longer change the earlier day. The train board flickered once more. Thomas put the letter away, then took it out again. In the growing light, the waiting room looked less like a place outside time. People were simply beginning their day there.

chapters.title: The Train That Changed Everything
pages: By seven, the station had taken on its daytime manners. The night cleaners had finished, though their work remained in the shine of the floor and the faint smell of soap near the doors. Commuters arrived with wet umbrellas and expressions of restrained complaint. A kiosk lifted its shutters. Somewhere behind the ticket hall, a coffee machine began grinding beans with an industriousness that made no distinction between an ordinary morning and a storm-delayed one.

The board continued to revise its account of the railway. Isabel’s train was listed, then marked delayed, then listed again with a new platform. Thomas’s service to Brünnfeld appeared below it. He stood to read the screen, letter in his inside pocket and case at his feet.
‘If they put it on the far platform, I shall need more time than the timetable allows,’ he said.

‘I’ll check the lift,’ Isabel replied. She went to the information point and found that one of the platform lifts had been taken out of service after water entered its shaft. The clerk gave her the accessible route by the main concourse, longer but open. She returned to Thomas with the details. He thanked her, then said, ‘I could have asked.’
‘You could.’
‘I am trying to discover whether accepting help makes me grateful or merely inconvenient.’
‘Perhaps it can be both.’
Thomas considered this, then laughed. ‘That is a historian’s answer. You leave room for contradictory evidence.’

A message came through on his phone. Elise had replied with a brief note: she was awake, she knew he was coming, and she would meet him at the station café if the train arrived. Thomas read it twice. The note offered neither forgiveness nor refusal. He looked relieved by the fact that it asked no one to pretend.
‘The café is on the other side of the station from the regional platforms,’ Isabel said. ‘You’ll have to cross back.’
‘I know. I can manage it.’ He said the words with quiet insistence, then added, ‘But I would be glad if you walked with me as far as the platform.’

She did. The train to Brünnfeld was announced with the caution of a service that had not fully recovered its confidence. Passengers gathered beneath the display. Thomas kept touching the edge of his case to make sure the letter was still inside. When the platform number appeared, Isabel walked with him through the main concourse, past the florist’s tulips and the coffee kiosk, taking the accessible route as they had been told.
At the platform, Thomas stopped beside a yellow line. ‘I don’t know what she will say.’
‘You don’t have to know before you go.’
‘That sounds annoyingly sensible.’
‘I’ve had practice since midnight.’

For a moment they looked at one another without needing to improve the exchange. Thomas offered his hand. Isabel shook it, and he boarded when the doors opened. The train pulled away slowly, its windows clouded with rain. She watched until it passed the end of the platform, not because she expected the departure to answer anything, but because seeing him choose mattered.

Her own service was still waiting. The board gave no firm time, only a notice that the eastern line remained restricted. The message she had left the person at her destination had received a reply: take the time you need; let me know when you can. The words did not repair the breakup or restore the job she had lost. They did not have to. They made room for the next honest thing.

Isabel bought coffee from the kiosk. It was too hot, a little bitter, and far better than Anna’s vending-machine cup. She stood by the tall windows, watching buses turn at the forecourt and water drip from the roof in steady threads. Across the river, the hospital windows caught the first clear light. Somewhere beyond them, the ordinary streets Anna had described were filling with people going to work, carrying laundry, buying bread.

The station was still a place of departures, but it no longer seemed designed to test whether she could face the world without help. She had asked a clerk, followed a nurse’s directions, listened to an old teacher revise a letter, and accepted that none of these actions had made the storm obey. Planning had brought her to Rosenstadt; it had not controlled what happened there.

When her train finally appeared on the board, it came with a further delay and a platform number. Isabel read the information once, then put her phone away. She had time to reach the platform. She also had time to miss something else. The thought no longer felt like a threat that required immediate argument.

She walked towards the stairs, carrying the empty bakery bag folded in her coat pocket. The rain had thinned to mist over the tracks. Beyond the glass, the city was not transformed, exactly. Its stones remained wet; its buses would still be late; its coffee was uneven. Yet Isabel had begun to see it not as scenery arranged around her journey, but as a place where people made mornings together, imperfectly and without applause.
At the platform entrance she turned once towards the station clock. It was still several minutes fast. This time, she did not check it again.

chapters.title: A Vacancy Made of Weather
pages: By the time Isabel reached the modest hotel on Karmeliter Street, rain had found its way beneath the collar of her coat. The sign above the door promised rooms and breakfast in three languages, though one of the letters had gone dark. Inside, the lobby smelled of wet wool, floor polish and coffee that had been left too long on its warmer. A brass umbrella stand held six umbrellas, all dripping into the same shallow dish.

The woman behind the desk checked the reservation book, then checked it again, as though the second inspection might improve the situation. She had silver beginning at her temples and a name badge that read ELENA FISCHER. ‘I’m afraid we’re full,’ she said. Her voice was courteous, but not soft. ‘There’s a trade fair, a concert, and what seems to be a convention of people who have all decided to arrive in Rosenstadt tonight.’
Isabel set her damp bag beside her feet. ‘I didn’t have a reservation.’

‘That does make things simpler,’ Elena replied. It was not quite a joke, though a small line appeared beside her mouth. ‘It also means I have no room to pretend I can find you one.’ She turned the book so Isabel could see the neat rows of names. ‘I can call two places across the river. I can’t promise they’ll answer, or that they’ll have anything.’

The rain tapped at the glass door, impatiently correcting the silence. Isabel thought of the station, the missed train, the plans she had kept adjusting as if a timetable were a moral document. ‘Please call.’

Elena reached for the telephone. The first guesthouse had no answer. The second had a room, but only if Isabel could reach it before midnight; its owner had already gone home and was returning to let in a late arrival. Elena gave Isabel the address and wrote down the tram and bus numbers. Then the desk phone rang.

She listened without interrupting. ‘Yes, I understand,’ she said. ‘No, I’m not asking you to keep it indefinitely.’ She put her hand over the receiver and looked at Isabel. ‘A cancellation. One room, but it is not available until the guest has checked out and the cleaner has finished. That may be half past six. You would need to wait somewhere until then.’
‘I can wait.’

‘You can wait in the lobby,’ Elena said, ‘provided you understand this is not a room and I cannot offer you one of the staff areas. I have a duty manager coming at seven. I’m not going to make an exception that causes trouble for the night porter.’ She said it plainly, without apology. ‘I can get you tea. There’s a bakery that opens early, two streets away. If the river bus is running, the stop is outside.’
The boundaries seemed, to Isabel, almost restful. Elena was not offering rescue; she was describing what could actually be done. ‘Tea would be good. Thank you.’

While Elena filled the kettle, Isabel took out her phone. A message from her project director had arrived while she was crossing the square: We need to discuss the presentation. The client expects your original proposal in person at nine. If you cannot attend, we may need to reassign the commission. Please call as soon as possible.

She read it once, then again, holding the phone low beside the steaming cup. The original plan required an early train from Rosenstadt and a meeting in another city. The train she had meant to take had gone without her. There might be a later connection, but the storm had delayed several services and the board at the station had been changing its mind in amber letters.
‘Bad news?’ Elena asked, setting down a small plate with two biscuits. She had not asked what Isabel was doing in Rosenstadt, and Isabel was grateful for that.
‘A decision dressed as a warning.’

Elena glanced at the message without trying to read it. ‘Those are popular in offices.’ Then she returned to the booking screen. Her kindness, Isabel understood, did not require her to become curious. She could make tea, offer a chair, and keep the hotel’s rules intact.

Isabel typed a reply, deleted it, and began again. She would not promise to appear at nine when she could not yet say how. Nor would she let the missed train decide the matter for her. Outside, the street lamps shone on the wet stones; the city looked less like an obstacle than a place that had not agreed to organise itself around her.

She sent a short message asking for a call at seven, and proposed presenting the work remotely if travel remained impossible. It was not the arrangement she had planned. It was also not surrender. When she put the phone away, her hands were still cold, but they had stopped trembling.

Elena brought a folded blanket from a cupboard. ‘For the chair, not the floor,’ she said. ‘And please leave the blanket here when you go. I spend half my week looking for things guests take by accident.’
‘I’ll try not to become part of your statistics.’
‘That would be considerate.’ Elena’s expression did not change, but this time the line at her mouth became a smile.

Isabel settled in the lobby chair, facing the dark window. The arrangement was temporary, uncomfortable, and honest. For the first time that night, she did not attempt to turn it into something more flattering.

chapters.title: The Man with the Unsent Call
pages: A little after one, the door opened and a man came in carrying a folded newspaper over his head. It had not helped. Water ran from the newspaper onto his dark coat, and from the coat onto the tiled floor. He paused to survey the lobby as though expecting it to issue a ruling.
‘The city has made a strong case for indoor life,’ he said.
Elena passed him a towel. ‘The city will be pleased to hear it.’

He gave his name as David Chen and asked whether there was a room. Elena repeated that the hotel was full, explained the cancellation expected at half past six, and made no attempt to soften the details. David listened with the attentive expression of someone accustomed to making other people feel heard. Then he looked at the empty chair opposite Isabel.
‘May I?’
‘It belongs to the hotel,’ Isabel said. ‘You should ask the hotel.’
Elena looked up from the computer. ‘You may sit there. You may not put your wet newspaper on the radiator. It leaves ink.’

David obeyed. He was perhaps in his late thirties, carefully dressed in clothes that had been chosen for a meeting rather than a storm. A narrow leather case rested against his leg. He set his phone on the table, screen upward, and then turned it face down.
‘Business?’ Isabel asked, before she could decide whether she meant to.

‘A meeting that was meant to be difficult and succeeded.’ He removed his glasses to wipe them. ‘I’m in transport investment. We spent three hours discussing a project that will be described in the morning as a productive exchange of views.’
‘Was it?’
‘No.’ He put the glasses back on. ‘But people like a phrase they can put in an email.’

He said this with the easy confidence of a man who knew the uses of a good sentence. Yet every few minutes he checked the dark screen of his phone. Isabel noticed the habit and then disliked herself for noticing it. She had spent much of the evening watching people’s faces for information they had not offered.
A notification lit the screen. David read it, did not reply, and turned the phone over again. The gesture was so deliberate that it seemed less like concealment than a small performance of control.
‘Are you waiting for someone?’ Isabel asked.
‘Not exactly.’ He lifted the newspaper and inspected a tear in its edge. ‘My partner and daughter are at home. I said I’d call when I knew whether I was taking the project.’
‘And do you know?’

‘I know what the project costs. The company wants a cheaper route through the eastern district, which means replacing two local stops with a shuttle service. The numbers are persuasive if you count time as money and leave out the people who will have to walk in the rain.’
‘And you don’t want to take it.’

‘I don’t want to be the man who recommends it. That is not quite the same thing as refusing it.’ David ran a thumb along the newspaper’s wet fold. ‘There are people in my firm who think I’m good at finding a compromise. I’m beginning to suspect this means I make bad decisions sound comfortable.’
Isabel thought of the message waiting on her phone. ‘A proposal can be changed.’
‘Of course.’ He glanced at her. ‘You say that as if you’ve recently discovered it.’
‘I’m trying not to let a missed connection make my decisions for me.’
He looked towards the window, where the reflected lights trembled across the glass. ‘That sounds sensible.’
‘It isn’t meant to sound sensible.’
For the first time, his polished manner slipped. He laughed once, quietly. ‘No. I suppose not.’
His phone lit again. This time the message preview showed only a name and a question: Are you coming home tomorrow? David stared at it, then put the phone in his pocket.
‘You could call,’ Isabel said.
‘I could.’
‘You could also decide about the project.’
‘You make difficult things sound like items on a list.’
‘I like lists.’
‘Yes,’ he said, without unkindness. ‘I had guessed.’
She felt the remark land where it was meant to. ‘And I’m guessing you like having the decision remain undecided. Then nobody can object to what you’ve done.’
David looked at her for a long moment. ‘You don’t know me.’
‘No.’ Isabel put both hands round her cup. ‘That’s why I’m guessing.’

His expression tightened, then eased. He did not thank her for the observation, which was perhaps a sign that he had heard it. Instead he asked Elena whether there was a place nearby where he could get a coffee. She told him the station café stayed open all night, though its coffee had recently become worse.
‘A rare endorsement,’ he said.
‘I’m paid to be accurate, not enthusiastic.’
David stood and gathered his case. At the door, he paused. ‘I’ll call home from the station. That is not a decision about the project.’
‘No,’ Isabel said. ‘It’s a call.’
He gave her a brief nod and went back into the rain.

The lobby settled around the sound of the closing door. Isabel looked at her own phone. The message from work remained unanswered beyond her request for a conversation. She had not solved the commission, and David had not solved his project or his family. Still, the night had made it harder to confuse postponement with care.

chapters.title: What Nadia Had Not Said
pages: Nadia arrived at the hotel shortly before three, carrying a canvas bag and an umbrella whose ribs had begun to bend. She came in quickly, as if the rain were following her through the door, then stopped when she saw Isabel awake in the chair.
‘I thought you’d found a room,’ she said.
‘A room may become available at half past six.’
‘That’s not the same thing.’ Nadia shook the umbrella over the mat. ‘But it’s better than the station.’

She had spent the last hour trying to arrange somewhere dry to stay, without success. The night buses were still running, though not regularly; one had taken her as far as the river, where she had walked through the storm rather than pay for a taxi she could not afford. She explained all this with a briskness that made the account sound almost cheerful.
‘You could have called me,’ Isabel said.
‘You were dealing with enough.’ Nadia took the chair beside her, leaving a careful space between them. ‘And I don’t like asking people to fix things.’
‘I wasn’t offering to fix it.’
‘You might have.’ Nadia tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear. ‘You’re very good at making a plan and then acting as if everyone else has been invited into it.’
Isabel could have defended herself. Instead she looked down at the paper cup in her hands. The coffee had gone cold and acquired a bitter skin.
‘That sounds familiar,’ she said.
‘It should.’ Nadia’s voice softened, but did not become gentle. ‘You do it because you care. It still leaves people standing outside the plan.’

The lobby clock advanced with a dry click. Somewhere upstairs a pipe knocked twice. Isabel remembered the route she had designed before the night began, every connection and alternative arranged so that she would never have to depend on anyone else.
‘I thought independence meant not needing help,’ she said.

‘That’s useful if you’re carrying a bag. Less useful if you’re trying to live with people.’ Nadia rubbed her palms together. ‘I used to say I was independent whenever I was afraid someone might say no.’
Isabel turned to her. Nadia’s eyes were on the window, not on her.
‘What are you afraid of?’

‘That I’ll go back and discover I’ve made a life I don’t want. Or that I’ll stay away and discover I left the parts I did want behind.’ She gave a small shrug. ‘Those are both quite ordinary fears. I’ve made them sound dramatic by carrying them around all night.’
‘You don’t have to decide tonight.’
‘Neither do you.’ Nadia glanced at Isabel’s phone. ‘But you do have to decide what you’ll tell your work people.’
‘I asked them to speak at seven. I’ve offered to present remotely if I can’t travel.’
‘That sounds like a new approach.’
‘It sounds like the only approach I can honestly promise.’
Nadia nodded. ‘Good. Don’t make honesty into a punishment, either.’

It was the sort of warning Isabel might once have treated as a criticism and set aside. Now she heard the care inside it without requiring Nadia to package that care neatly. She also heard the boundary: Nadia was not volunteering to guide her through every choice.
‘Would you like tea?’ Isabel asked.
‘Yes. If Elena says it’s allowed.’
From behind the desk, Elena said, ‘Tea is allowed. Sleeping in the breakfast room is not.’
‘I wasn’t planning to,’ Nadia replied.
‘Excellent. Then we understand one another.’
Elena made two cups and placed them on the low table. Nadia wrapped both hands round hers, then watched the steam vanish against the window.
‘I’m sorry I made you feel outside the plan,’ Isabel said.
Nadia considered this. ‘Thank you. I’m not sure I want an apology to become another plan.’
‘It won’t.’
‘We’ll see.’ Her mouth lifted at one corner. ‘I’m not very good at easy forgiveness.’
‘I wouldn’t trust you if you were.’

For a moment they sat without filling the space between them. Outside, a night bus passed, its windows bright and empty. The river beyond the buildings moved unseen, but Isabel could hear its low wash when the wind turned.

She understood that asking for help did not mean handing someone else the steering wheel. Nor did refusing help prove that she could manage alone. The distinction was quieter than she had expected. It did not make her feel brave; it made her feel less busy pretending.
Nadia leaned back and closed her eyes. ‘Wake me if the room appears.’
‘I will.’
‘And if I’m asleep, wake me anyway. I reserve the right to complain.’
Isabel smiled. ‘That seems fair.’
The two women drank the hotel’s tea while rain moved steadily down the glass. Neither promised that the morning would settle what the night had disturbed.

chapters.title: A Message from the Other Bank
pages: At four, Thomas appeared in the lobby with his collar turned up and one sleeve darker than the other. He carried no umbrella. He looked surprised to find Isabel there, then unsurprised that he was surprised.
‘You’re still awake,’ he said.
‘So are you.’
‘I have less excuse.’ He glanced at Nadia, who had opened one eye but had not sat up. ‘Am I interrupting?’
‘Only the tea,’ Nadia said. ‘It can bear it.’

Thomas sat on the edge of the chair nearest the door. He had always seemed to Isabel a man who preferred the margins of rooms: close enough to leave without ceremony, close enough to hear what was being said. His phone was in his hand, its screen lit with a message.
‘An old friend has written,’ he said. ‘I haven’t heard from him in years.’
‘Good news?’ Isabel asked.
‘A question, mostly.’ He turned the phone over. ‘He’s in Brno. His wife has gone back to her sister’s, and he wants to know if I’ll meet him for lunch. He says he needs to talk.’
‘Will you go?’ Nadia asked.
Thomas rubbed at a rain mark on his cuff. ‘I don’t know. The last time we spoke, I told him I was tired of being the person he called after he’d made a mess of things.’
‘Perhaps you still are,’ Nadia said.
‘Perhaps.’ He looked down at his hands. ‘I also miss him. Those facts don’t cancel each other out, which would be convenient.’

There was no grand confession in his voice. He sounded irritated, above all, by the inconvenience of affection. Isabel recognised the irritation; it had often been easier to blame the shape of a problem than to admit she wanted something inside it.
‘You don’t have to promise him anything,’ she said. ‘You can answer the question he asked.’
Thomas glanced up. ‘You’ve become very good at offering limited advice.’
‘I’m practising.’
He read the message once more. Then he typed a reply, stopped, and erased it. Nadia shifted in her chair.
‘If you don’t want to meet him, don’t go because you feel guilty,’ she said. ‘If you do, don’t pretend it means everything is repaired.’
‘You make reconciliation sound like plumbing.’
‘I make it sound like a thing that needs maintenance.’

Thomas gave a small laugh. He typed again, slower. He told his friend he would meet him for lunch, but that he could not promise to make the old arguments disappear. He read the message aloud before sending it, as if the words might become more dependable when heard.
‘That’s clear,’ Isabel said.
‘It’s also rather cold.’
‘Those aren’t opposites.’
He sent it. The phone made no sound, and there was no reply. Thomas put it away with an expression that held relief and regret in equal measure.
‘Well,’ he said, ‘now I have a lunch to attend or cancel.’
‘A very modest beginning,’ Nadia said.
‘My favourite kind.’

Elena came from the back office with a clipboard. She said the cancelled room was not ready yet and would not be ready sooner merely because everyone in the lobby was tired. She did, however, point out that the bakery on the corner had turned its sign to OPEN.
‘They have good rolls,’ she said. ‘Their coffee is adequate if you don’t ask it to be anything else.’
‘You set a high standard,’ Thomas said.
‘I set an accurate one.’

They went out together. The rain had thinned to a cold mist, and the stones shone as if someone had polished them during the night. A delivery van stood at the kerb, its back doors open. The bakery windows glowed a muted gold in the blue-grey street.

The bakery was narrow and warm. Its counter was crowded with poppy-seed rolls, small loaves and trays of pastries that released a sweet, browned smell each time the oven door opened. The woman serving them spoke little and moved quickly. Her white apron was marked with flour at the hip.

Thomas bought bread for himself and, after a moment’s thought, an extra roll. He did not say who it was for. Nadia ordered coffee and complained that it was too hot; she drank it anyway. Isabel chose a plain roll and ate it standing by the window.

Across the street, the first city bus moved through the mist. Its headlights stretched over the wet road and vanished at the next crossing. The ordinary morning was beginning without asking permission from anyone.
‘He may not answer,’ Thomas said, looking at his phone.
‘He may not,’ Isabel agreed.
‘I thought you’d tell me it didn’t matter.’
‘It matters. It just doesn’t tell you what to do next.’
Thomas looked at her, then gave a short nod. He tucked the extra roll into his coat pocket, where it would probably be flattened before lunch.
For once, Isabel had no urge to improve the moment by naming its lesson. She finished her bread, wiped a crumb from her glove, and watched the city grow visible around them.

chapters.title: The Approach That Was Not a Route
pages: At six thirty, Elena called Isabel’s name from behind the desk. The room was ready. It was small, overlooking the side street rather than the river, and the radiator clicked as if it were uncertain about its responsibilities. Isabel set down her bag but did not take off her coat. She had a call at seven.

Nadia stayed in the lobby with Thomas. David had not returned from the station café, and there was no sign that he had made his call home. Isabel wondered whether she should have asked more directly. Then she remembered that she had already said what she could say without taking his decision away from him.
The project director answered on the second ring. His voice had the measured briskness of a man who had been awake for an hour and wanted everyone else to know it.
‘We need the presentation,’ he said. ‘The client has arranged the whole morning around it.’
‘I understand. The storm has disrupted the rail service. I can’t promise I’ll reach you in time.’
‘You planned this journey.’
‘I did.’

There was a pause. Isabel imagined him looking at the same document they had both reviewed, with its exact timings and carefully labelled alternatives. ‘The client is not interested in the weather,’ he said.
‘Then they may be interested in the work.’
‘That is a confident distinction.’

‘It is the distinction I can offer.’ She looked at the room’s narrow window. Beyond it, a woman in a red scarf pushed a bicycle through the wet street. ‘I can present the key material by video. More importantly, I can change the proposal. The original route assumes that the audience will arrive from the central station in a single wave. The delays here have shown me how fragile that assumption is. I’d like to include a second arrival pattern and a simpler way to redirect people when connections fail.’
‘You’re proposing to revise the work overnight?’
‘I’m proposing that we show the client what the work has failed to account for.’
He exhaled. ‘If they don’t accept it, the commission may be withdrawn.’
‘I know.’
‘And if you aren’t in the room, someone else will have to present.’
‘Then let them. I can send the new material now and join remotely. If that isn’t acceptable, I understand that you’ll need to reassign it.’

Her voice remained steady, though she could feel her pulse at the base of her throat. She had expected that making a choice would produce a feeling of certainty. Instead it produced a narrow, practical discomfort. She had chosen what she could stand behind; the consequences remained outside her control.
‘You’re asking for a great deal of trust,’ he said.
‘I’m asking you to judge the proposal.’
Another pause. Then he said he would review the revised pages with the client and send her a link for the call. It was not a promise that the commission would stay hers. It was also not a refusal.
After they hung up, Isabel sat on the edge of the bed. The room was quiet except for the radiator and the distant wash of traffic. She opened her laptop and began to revise.

The first draft had made the journey look clean. A line began at the station and led, without hesitation, to the meeting place. There were no delays, no wet coats, no children asking where the bus had gone, and no tired traveller looking at a sign that had changed twice in five minutes. Isabel had called this clarity. Now she saw that it was partly omission.

She added a second route, then a third. Not an elaborate web of instructions, but a point where a person could ask for help and receive a useful answer. The design allowed for missed connections without pretending they could always be prevented. It was less elegant than the original plan. It was also more generous.
At the lobby desk, Elena was sorting keys into a drawer. ‘Your room is available until eleven,’ she said. ‘After that, I need it for the next arrival.’
‘Understood.’
‘Breakfast is served downstairs from seven. The bread is better than the coffee.’
‘That seems to be the standard opinion.’
‘I don’t run the bakery.’ Elena closed the drawer. ‘I only report on it.’

Isabel went back upstairs. At seven twenty, her revised pages were ready. The video call began at seven thirty. Her director appeared first, then the client’s two representatives, both framed against pale office walls. They listened while Isabel explained the changes. One asked whether the added route would increase costs. Another wanted to know who would maintain the new information point.

Isabel answered what she could. She did not pretend the questions were minor, and she did not claim that one difficult night had made her an expert on the city. She described the specific failure she had seen and the limits of the solution she was proposing.
The client asked for time to consider it. The director ended the call without offering an opinion. Isabel closed the laptop and sat still for a few seconds.

In the lobby, Nadia was awake and drinking tea. Thomas stood by the window with his phone in his hand. He had received no answer from his friend, but had decided to keep the lunch appointment on his calendar.
‘How did it go?’ Nadia asked.
‘They’re considering it.’
‘That’s not an answer.’
‘No. It’s what happened.’

Nadia nodded, accepting the difference. Isabel picked up her bag. Outside, a bus went towards the river, its windows clouded with warmth. The storm had moved east, leaving the stones dark and shining. Somewhere beyond the roofs, trains were beginning to run on altered schedules.

Isabel had not recovered the journey she meant to take. She had not secured the commission, reconciled anyone, or turned uncertainty into a neat conclusion. What had changed was smaller and more useful: she could make a plan without mistaking it for a guarantee, and she could ask for help without calling herself dependent.
At the door she looked back at Elena, who was already answering a question from the next guest. ‘Thank you for the room.’
‘You’re welcome,’ Elena said. Then, as if to keep the exchange properly sized, she added, ‘Please leave the key on the desk.’
Isabel placed it beside the ledger and stepped into the morning.

chapters.title: The Bakery Opens on the Corner
pages: By the time Isabel left the guesthouse, the rain had thinned to a silver mist. It still shone on the pavements, but the storm had moved east, leaving the sky the colour of unpolished pewter. She had slept for perhaps two hours. The rest of the night had been spent listening to pipes knock in the wall and thinking of the train she had missed, as if the railway might eventually offer an explanation.

The street descended towards the river. Shutters were lifting one by one; a delivery van stood with its hazard lights blinking into the wet. At the corner, the bakery had opened. Warmth and the smell of yeast reached the pavement before Isabel reached the door.

Inside, a woman in a flour-marked apron was setting loaves on a wooden shelf. The glass was clouded with steam. A young man in a dark work jacket waited at the counter, counting coins in his palm. He looked at the paper bag beside him, then at the clock.
“You can have the last rye loaf,” the baker told him. “Unless you need it to be prettier.”
“I need it to be cheaper,” he said. “But I suppose rye has its principles.”
He paid, took the loaf and left without looking at the rain. Isabel ordered coffee and a small roll. The baker placed both on a tray, then noticed the overnight bag at Isabel’s feet.
“You were caught in it?” she asked.
“I was caught by the timetable.”
“That is worse. Weather usually admits it has done something.”

Isabel smiled. She took her coffee to the narrow counter by the window. Beyond the glass, a bus moved through the street, its windows lit and empty. It was too early for the usual noise of the city. A man hosed grit from the step of a pharmacy; a cyclist leaned over a lock, patiently working at it with a key.

She had once thought a good plan was one that left nothing to chance. Now she understood the weakness in that definition. A plan could be a useful shape for the day, but it could not make the day promise obedience. Nor could the failure of a plan be turned, by sheer force of will, into a different kind of success.
The baker returned with a clean cloth and wiped the counter beside her. “Station?” she asked.
“Eventually.”
“Then eat before you go. People at stations make poor decisions when they are hungry. They buy coffee that tastes of burnt rope and believe signs that say ‘temporary platform change’.”
“You sound experienced.”
“I have a brother who travels.” She glanced towards the door. “He has been travelling for twelve years. I have been hearing about it for twelve years.”

It was not a confession, exactly, and Isabel did not ask for one. She ate the roll while it was still warm. The butter had softened into the crumb. For a few minutes she was not a traveller or a writer with an appointment to salvage; she was simply a woman at a bakery counter, holding a cup between her hands while the city opened.
When she stood, the baker wrapped a second roll in paper.
“For the train,” she said. “It is not a gift. You have paid for breakfast.”
Isabel had not paid for the second roll, but she understood that arguing might cost more than accepting it. She placed a coin on the counter.

Outside, the mist lifted in fragments. She turned towards the river, where the stone embankment waited below the street. The bakery door shut softly behind her, and the smell of bread followed her for several steps.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Case
pages: The river was high but no longer rising. Brown water pushed past the piers, carrying twigs and a pale branch that turned slowly in the current. Along the embankment, the stone was dark with rain. A municipal worker in orange trousers cleared leaves from a drain with a short-handled rake, pausing whenever a bus crossed the bridge above him.

Isabel walked upstream. At the lower bridge, commuters had begun to gather in small, purposeful groups. They held their collars closed and stepped around the shallow pools without breaking conversation. A woman in a red scarf read a message while walking; a man with a briefcase held his newspaper above his head, though there was no rain left to keep off.

Nadia stood near the steps with her instrument case upright between her shoes. She was speaking to a station clerk on her phone, her voice controlled in the way people become controlled when they are trying not to sound worried.
“No, I understand the reservation,” she said. “I am asking whether the case can travel in the same carriage. It is not a second passenger.”
She listened, then closed her eyes briefly. “Yes. I know what the dimensions are.”
Isabel stopped a few paces away. Nadia ended the call and looked at her.
“They have found a way to charge me for the space beside me,” Nadia said. “I should admire the imagination.”
“Is it the case that is the problem, or the ticket?”
“The ticket permits one large item. This is larger than their definition of large.” Nadia tapped the case with two fingers. “It is a practical distinction, apparently.”

A couple of people moved around them towards the bridge. Isabel looked at the case, then at Nadia’s printed ticket, which she held folded in one hand. The instrument was valuable, but Nadia had already been told what the rules were. Isabel did not want to offer a solution that belonged only to her own confidence.
“Would you like me to look at the ticket with you?” she asked.
Nadia’s expression shifted, almost too slightly to notice. “Yes. If you don’t mind.”

They stepped beneath the bridge arch, out of the open wind. Isabel read the small print. The ticket was for a later train than Nadia had first intended to take; the luggage conditions were printed on the reverse, but the wording referred to musical instruments only if they were packed in a soft case. Isabel pointed this out.
“Mine is not soft,” Nadia said. “It has survived two border crossings and one very bad hotel lift.”
“Could the attendant make an exception if you paid for the neighbouring seat?”
“The train is full.”
“Then perhaps the luggage desk can register it before boarding. The ticket office opens at six.”
Nadia gave a dry laugh. “I was hoping you had found a secret railway.”
“No. Only a desk with a sign.”

That, at least, was useful. They checked the time on Isabel’s phone. The station was a short walk away, and the ticket office should be opening now. Nadia lifted the case. Isabel picked up the smaller bag without asking, then waited for Nadia to decide whether to let her carry it.
“Thank you,” Nadia said. “The case is mine. The bag is not important.”

They crossed the bridge together. On the far side, the river narrowed between buildings, reflecting a strip of pale sky. Nadia walked quickly, but she did not rush. She had the careful stride of someone measuring each step against the weight she carried.
At the station entrance, she took her bag from Isabel. “I can manage from here.”
“All right.”

The words felt different from an offer of rescue. Isabel let them stand. Nadia went through the doors with her case, and Isabel followed at a distance, not because Nadia needed her to, but because both of them were going to the same place.

chapters.title: The First Boards
pages: The station had changed during the night. The hard shine of the wet floor remained, but the building no longer seemed to belong to the storm. Commuters moved through it carrying paper cups and folded umbrellas. The departure boards clicked from one minute to the next. Somewhere behind the ticket windows, a printer began its steady mechanical chatter.

Nadia joined the short queue at the luggage desk. Isabel stood beside her, holding the paper bag from the bakery. When they reached the counter, the clerk examined the instrument case and then the ticket.
“It can go in the designated rack,” he said. “There is a handling charge.”
Nadia named the amount before he did. “I was told it would be more.”
“That was for the express service.” He slid a form across the counter. “This is for the ordinary train.”
“The ordinary train is the one I wanted.”

The clerk looked at her, uncertain whether this was a complaint. Nadia signed the form and paid. Isabel did not intervene. There was no need. The problem had been made smaller by a rule that turned out to be less absolute than the first answer, but Nadia had done the work of asking again.
She folded the receipt into the pocket of her coat. “I was prepared to argue with the clerk who wasn’t here.”
“That might have been satisfying.”
“For about a minute.”

They stood near a column while the crowd thickened. Nadia would leave from platform six; Isabel’s train was due on platform three. The station clock showed six minutes past six. A cleaner pushed a wide brush across the floor, gathering grit into a dark line.
“You’ll be all right with the case?” Isabel asked.
“Yes. They have given me a label, which means it has become official.” Nadia looked towards the platforms. “I am sorry about last night. I was difficult.”
“You were tired.”
“That is usually when I am most convinced that I am right.”
Isabel thought of the messages she had not sent, the plans she had kept polished for so long that she had mistaken them for decisions. “I know something about that.”
Nadia nodded, accepting the answer without turning it into a speech. “I hope your meeting goes well.”
“I’m not sure it will happen in the form I expected.”
“That may be a relief.”
“Or a problem.”
“Usually both.”
They smiled, though neither tried to make the moment last. Nadia shifted the handle of her case. “I have to find my platform.”
“So do I.”

At the foot of the stairs, they said goodbye. Nadia’s was a brief touch on Isabel’s sleeve, warm through the damp fabric. Then she moved into the stream of passengers with her case rolling steadily behind her. Isabel watched until the crowd divided them. She did not follow.

Her phone vibrated. The commissioner’s name appeared above the unfinished message she had drafted during the night. She stepped aside to let a family pass and read it once more. The original appointment was impossible now. She could blame the storm, the missed connection, the confusion of the station. All of those things were true, but they would not explain what she wanted next.

She deleted the sentence that began with I regret to inform you. In its place she wrote that she would not arrive in time for the agreed meeting. She acknowledged that this might change the commission, then proposed a different project: a short book about the city’s working mornings, made through conversations with people who did not appear in visitor guides. She asked whether they could speak by telephone the following week. She did not promise that the new idea was better. She did say it was hers.
She read the message, changed one word, and sent it.

The departure board clicked again. Isabel went down to platform three, where the train waited with its doors open. She bought a coffee from a kiosk and discovered it was not burnt rope, only disappointingly weak. There was no lesson in this. She drank it anyway.

chapters.title: A Seat Facing Forward
pages: The morning train was already half full. Isabel found a seat beside the window and set her overnight bag on the rack. The bakery roll lay in its paper beside her notebook. Across the aisle, a man in a grey coat was trying to fit a bicycle helmet beneath his seat; a child watched him with the grave attention usually reserved for animals.

The doors closed. The train waited for a moment, then drew away from Rosenstadt. The station slid past in sections: the waiting room windows, the platform lamps, a porter closing the door of the luggage office. Beyond the tracks, the city gathered itself against the low sky.

Isabel watched the river appear between warehouses. From this angle it seemed narrower than it had on foot, though the water was still carrying the storm east. The bridge came next, then the roofs, then a strip of wet pavement where a night bus had left its blue reflection in a puddle.

She opened her notebook. The old pages were full of routes, timings and neat columns. In the margin beside the first timetable she had written, in blue ink, a question about how much could be fitted into one day. She had not answered it. Perhaps the question had been asking the wrong thing.

Marta had understood the value of ordinary work without insisting that it was noble. Lukas had not made the missed connection disappear; he had shown that a person could be kind without arranging the ending. Nadia had carried her own case, and still accepted help with the lesser bag. Thomas had chosen what to do with his morning without offering a reason for every part of himself. Elena and David remained complicated in Isabel’s thoughts; Anna’s words, too, would not settle into a clean instruction.

They were not all lessons, and they were not all hers to keep. The night had given her better questions, not easy answers. That distinction mattered. She had spent years believing that independence meant asking nobody to interfere. Now she suspected it might mean being honest about what she could manage, and what she could not, without making either fact a verdict.

Her phone remained quiet. The commissioner might refuse the new proposal, or accept it with conditions. The missed appointment would still have consequences. She was not relieved of them simply because she had found a more truthful way to describe the morning.

At the next stop, passengers climbed aboard carrying damp coats and small paper parcels. A woman sat opposite Isabel and placed a jar of flowers on the floor. The glass had fogged. Neither woman spoke. The train moved on.

Isabel took out her pen. She wrote the names of several streets she had passed on foot, then crossed out the phrase a city revealed. It was too grand and too certain. She replaced it with a note about opening hours: the bakery at six, the river steps at dawn, the ticket desk when the first commuters arrived. Those details did not explain Rosenstadt, but they gave her somewhere to begin.

The carriage rocked over a set of points. Her coffee tipped against the cup lid but did not spill. She steadied it with her palm, amused by how quickly she had reached to prevent even this small disorder.

Outside, the rooftops gave way to gardens and wet fields. Isabel ate the roll. It had lost its warmth, but the rye was good and the crust held firm. She thought of the room above the bar, the waiting room clock, the nurse at dawn, the silence after questions that no one had been ready to answer. She thought of the station, too, and the train she had missed. Not as a turning point ordained for her, but as a fact that had altered the available route.
When the conductor came to check her ticket, she found it at once. That pleased her, though she knew it proved very little.
She closed the notebook, then opened it again and added a line at the bottom of the page: Ask before deciding what the answer will be.

The train gathered speed. Isabel leaned back, facing forward, with the next city still unnamed in her mind. She had a message sent, a meeting to renegotiate and a book that might not be commissioned. There was no promise that these beginnings would lead anywhere. For the first time in a long while, she could let that remain unknown without mistaking it for failure.
